Ethics approval is typically not required for theoretical work, simulations, reviews, meta-analyses, or secondary analyses of published data.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

table.formatted: Across models, the correlation between the masculine association of a term and its concreteness was negative (mean r = -0.174; 95% confidence interval (CI) across models = -0.205 to -0.142; range across models = -0.233 to -0.066; t(11) = -12.03; P = 1.1 × 10 -7 ; two-tailed one-sample t-test across models), and it was negative and significant after Bonferroni correction in 12 of 12 models (n = 85,229 to 102,842 terms per model; two-tailed Pearson's correlations; Supplementary Table <ref type="table">11</ref>; 'Statistical Analysis of Textual Data and Robustness Tests' in Materials and Methods).

table.formatted: Four assignment schemes are compared. (i) Primary sense, the main-text rule: each word receives the single domain of its first-listed WordNet sense within its dominant part of speech. (ii) All senses, the rule of Supplementary Section 10: a word joins every domain in which it has a sense within its dominant part of speech, so a polysemous word can contribute to several domains. (iii) Domain-unambiguous words only: the analysis is restricted to the 16,553 words whose senses all fall in a single domain, for which assignment is beyond dispute and the primary/all-sense distinction vanishes. report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = c("P < 0.05", "P < 0.05", "P ≤ 0.014", 
"P < 0.05"), Text = c("; P < 0.05 in 15 domains; two-tailed paired t-tests across 12 models).", 
"; P < 0.05 in 29 domains; 12 models).", "Recomputing the nine panel correlations with membership restricted to each word's primary sense (on the common single-word vocabulary; the panel sample sizes in Supplementary Table 17 additionally include two-word artifact entries), every correlation remained negative, ranging from r = -0.05 (text-embedding-3-large, artifact nouns; n = 2,266) to r = -0.24 (Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B, acts of communication; n = 630), all two-tailed P ≤ 0.014.", 
"Domains, WordNet domains with at least 100 assigned words (noun.person excluded); Abstract > concrete, domains with a positive gap, with the two-tailed binomial sign-test P; Sig. +/-, domains whose gap is significantly positive/negative at P < 0.05 (two-tailed one-sample t-tests across the 12 models)."
)), row.names = c(NA, -4L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"
))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("P = 0.31", "P = 0.47", "P = 0.31"), Sentence = c("In all five languages the correlation is negative (Supplementary Table 10): Turkish (r = -0.244; 95% CI = -0.320 to -0.165), Italian (-0.187; -0.243 to -0.129), French (-0.118; -0.166 to -0.070), Portuguese (-0.039; -0.071 to -0.008; P = 0.015) and Indonesian (-0.027; -0.079 to 0.025; P = 0.31).", "For words and phrases pooled, the mean correlation was -0.073 (95% CI = -0.101 to -0.044; t(11) = -5.63; P = 1.5 × 10 -4 ; negative in 12 of 12 models and significantly so in 11, the exception being BERT, r = -0.002, P = 0.47).", "For comparison, the corresponding mean correlation for the words alone (Fig. 1c) was -0.067 (95% CI = -0.095 to -0.039; negative in 12 of 12 models and significantly so in 11; the exception was GPT2, r = -0.005, P = 0.31)." )), row.names = c(NA, -3L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. info.title: The Male Abstraction Bias in Internet Culture and Large Language Models

text.text: Conceptual abstraction and gender are two equally central aspects of the human mind, yet they have traditionally been studied in isolation from one another, as though they were fundamentally separate.

Here, we find gender and abstraction are systematically linked throughout the space of concepts spanning single (N = 40,000) and multi-word expressions (N = 67,000): across billions of words and millions of images on the internet -and across numerous measurement techniques, including human and AI classifications -more abstract concepts are more associated with men, a pattern we show replicates in languages around the world.

This male abstraction bias not only holds across semantic domains, but it also maps onto grammatical structure: verbs and adverbs are more abstract and more male-coded, revealing a system-wide trace of stereotypes accentuating agentic qualities in men.

Furthermore, we show this bias readily emerges in the free associations humans and AIs produce in controlled online tasks, indicating its psychological internalization and its algorithmic reproduction.

These findings identify a latent structure in conceptual space that unifies a range of stereotypes: for example, framings of women as more embodied, emotional, and warm, versus men as more cognitive, rational, and competent; as well as erroneous views of men as better at mathematics, science, and engineering.

More broadly, by analyzing an unprecedently large, multimodal sample of online data, we provide culture-wide evidence of gender as a core organizing principle shaping conceptual space far beyond the characterization of people and social roles.
Gender stereotypes are primarily studied as biased beliefs about people and social roles: who is warm, who is competent, who belongs in science.
Here, we show that gender runs far deeper, organizing the structure of concepts themselves.
Across billions of words and millions of images online, spanning 100,000 common words and phrases, we find that more abstract (concrete) concepts are systematically more associated with men (women).

This male abstraction bias replicates across semantic domains and languages, maps onto fundamental grammar (verbs and adverbs are more abstract and male-coded), and surfaces in the free associations of humans and large language models.
These findings reveal a hidden structure in conceptual space that unifies many stereotypes, a structure AI is learning and reproducing.
Does social identity shape the foundational structure of concepts?

Traditionally, cognitive science has examined the structure of human concepts by identifying computational principles and constraints operating in the individual's mind [1] [2] [3] [4] [5] , treating social factors as inputs that shape concept learninge.g., by influencing exposure to and adoption of concepts -rather than as constituents of conceptual structure itself.
text.formatted: Traditionally, cognitive science has examined the structure of human concepts by identifying computational principles and constraints operating in the individual's mind <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref> <ref type="bibr">[2]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5]</ref> , treating social factors as inputs that shape concept learninge.g., by influencing exposure to and adoption of concepts -rather than as constituents of conceptual structure itself.

text.text: This is especially the case when considering the most foundational dimensions of concepts like abstractness, taxonomic hierarchy, and statistical inference.

For example, the abstractness of concepts is often defined by how easy it is to perceive and physically interact with the referents for a given category (e.g., "chairs" are more concrete and perceivable, whereas "beliefs" and "nations" are more abstract), such that decades of work have argued that various individual-level factors relating to cognitive efficiency skew concepts toward an optimal middle-range ("basic level") of abstraction 1, 2, [6] [7] [8] .

text.text: While recent accounts explore the social grounding of abstract concepts, they focus on social interaction as the route by which abstract concepts are acquired and stabilized 9 , rather than on whether social information (e.g., relating to identity) shapes conceptual abstraction itself.

text.text: By contrast, aspects of human cognition relating to personal identity, such as gender and race, are often viewed as socially constructed and historically contingent, and as thus belonging to emergent communication and cultural dynamics, rather than to the foundations of conceptual structure 10, 11 .

text.text: However, recent work has discovered numerous ways in which gender influences various cognitive processes, from logical reasoning and emotion to the perception of everyday objects [12] [13] [14] , suggesting that gender may play a more foundational role in conceptual structure than has been previously recognized 15 .

text.text: Here, we investigate whether abstraction and gender are systematically and structurally linked throughout the space of human concepts.
A key challenge in the study of concept abstractness is the disconnect between formal definitions and human judgements.

Initially, cognitive science defined abstractness via hierarchical generality 16, 17 ; a superset like "animal" is more abstract than its subset "dog", which is more abstract than its subset "border collies", with each step down the tree restricting the range of referents.
text.formatted: Initially, cognitive science defined abstractness via hierarchical generality <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">16,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">17</ref> ; a superset like "animal" is more abstract than its subset "dog", which is more abstract than its subset "border collies", with each step down the tree restricting the range of referents.

text.text: However, a large body of work has since found that human judgments depart from this hierarchical definition of concept generality [18] [19] [20] .
text.formatted: However, a large body of work has since found that human judgments depart from this hierarchical definition of concept generality <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">[18]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[19]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[20]</ref> .

text.text: In a now classic study, Brysbaert et al. 21 recruited many human participants to evaluate the 40,000 most common concepts in the English language in terms of how concrete or abstract they are.

text.text: Not infrequently, general concepts like "animal" were rated as concrete, whereas specific concepts like "string theory" (a narrow subset of all scientific theories) were evaluated as abstract.
This led cognitive scientists to distinguish hierarchical generality ('concept specificity') from the concreteness-abstractness continuum 18, 19 .
text.formatted: This led cognitive scientists to distinguish hierarchical generality ('concept specificity') from the concreteness-abstractness continuum <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">18,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">19</ref> .

text.text: In the current view, concrete concepts are those whose referents are easily perceivable and imageable (e.g., a "rock" or a "house"), while abstract concepts lack clear and perceivable sensory structure (e.g., "justice" and "knowledge") [21] [22] [23] [24] .
text.formatted: In the current view, concrete concepts are those whose referents are easily perceivable and imageable (e.g., a "rock" or a "house"), while abstract concepts lack clear and perceivable sensory structure (e.g., "justice" and "knowledge") <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">[21]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">[22]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">[23]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">[24]</ref> .

text.text: The limitations of relying on human subjective judgments notwithstanding 25 , research spanning over a decade has found that judgments of concept concreteness-abstractness are not only reliable across raters and replicable across languages 26, 27 , and closely approximated by large language models 28 , but are also predictive of several conceptual features and processes, including language acquisition 29 , sentence processing 30 , emotion 31 , metaphor 32, 33 , and persuasion 34, 35.

text.text: Despite the minimal cross-pollination between the study of conceptual abstraction and gender, recurring themes across widespread stereotypes suggest that concept concreteness and abstractness may be deeply tied to gender associations.

A number of popular gender stereotypes skew toward associating women with more concrete, embodied qualities, such as emotions and interpersonal warmth 13, [36] [37] [38] [39] , while associating men with more abstract qualities like reasoning, problem solving, and competence 12, 37, 38, 40 .
text.formatted: A number of popular gender stereotypes skew toward associating women with more concrete, embodied qualities, such as emotions and interpersonal warmth <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">13,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">[36]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">[37]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">[38]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">[39]</ref> , while associating men with more abstract qualities like reasoning, problem solving, and competence <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">12,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">37,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">38,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">40</ref> .

text.text: This generalizes to stereotypes related to occupational sorting in which men are (falsely) assumed to be more competent in math and STEM disciplines than women [41] [42] [43] , skewing people toward assuming men are more qualified for highly cognitive, knowledge work.
text.formatted: This generalizes to stereotypes related to occupational sorting in which men are (falsely) assumed to be more competent in math and STEM disciplines than women <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">[41]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">[42]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">[43]</ref> , skewing people toward assuming men are more qualified for highly cognitive, knowledge work.

text.text: Importantly, prior work has focused on a definition of stereotypes as directly connected to social roles, with a focus on domain-specific biases and patterns of discrimination (e.g., hiring biases in STEM fields).

However, this leaves open the question of whether stereotypes are primarily byproducts of role dynamics in these social contexts (e.g., normative biases in the kinds of work women and men are expected and hired to do), or whether these domain-specific role judgments are extensions of deeper, more general gender biases in the structure of concepts themselves, and specifically in systematic differences between concrete and abstract concepts.

This question is important because while stereotyped role dynamics may be possible to shift in particular contexts (e.g., by increasing women's leadership in organizations 44 ), if gender is structurally entangled with abstraction as a fundamental structure throughout human concepts, including our most basic and common notions, this suggests the challenge of achieving enduring changes in gender inequality may require far more fundamental shifts in human thought and culture.

text.text: In this direction, a developing stream of research in social psychology has begun to identify ways in which abstractness may be related to gender.

However, much of this literature is based on construal level theory (CLT) 45, 46 which defines abstractness as psychological distance -e.g., via the level of spatial, temporal, or social distance between an observer and what is being described -and thus is not directly related to or engaged with questions about concept abstractness and conceptual structure specifically, since it relates more to the stance of the observer rather than to the concepts themselves.
text.formatted: However, much of this literature is based on construal level theory (CLT) <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">45,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">46</ref> which defines abstractness as psychological distance -e.g., via the level of spatial, temporal, or social distance between an observer and what is being described -and thus is not directly related to or engaged with questions about concept abstractness and conceptual structure specifically, since it relates more to the stance of the observer rather than to the concepts themselves.

text.text: Nevertheless, using CLT, Joshi et al. 47 show-across a meta-analysis of experiments, a corpus of blog posts, and the floor speech of members of the US Congress-that men tend to describe their experiences and work in more abstract language than women.
text.formatted: Nevertheless, using CLT, Joshi et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">47</ref> show-across a meta-analysis of experiments, a corpus of blog posts, and the floor speech of members of the US Congress-that men tend to describe their experiences and work in more abstract language than women.

text.text: Dodson et al. 48 similarly draw from CLT across six preregistered studies to show that people implicitly associate women's names with low-construal terms and men's names with high-construal terms, and that they describe women as more concrete than abstract and men as more abstract than concrete, both in general and across 48 occupations-although in one study women were also described as more abstract than men.

text.text: Otherwise, in a recent opinion piece, Bailey and Leshin 49 argue that, absent an explicit gender frame, people represent women specifically as women but represent men as generic people, such that men come to be associated with a wider variety of referents and attributes 50 ; although the authors do not frame this asymmetry in terms of abstractness, it maps onto concept specificity-the breadth of referents a category subsumes-which is related to, but empirically separable from, rated concreteness 18, 19 .

text.text: Notably, Bailey and Leshin 49 evaluate the construal-level stereotypes 48 from prior work as an instance of 'balanced' gender representation-women as one thing, men as its complement-that is distinct from the categorical asymmetry they propose, with women represented as one thing and men as many.

text.text: Overall, despite these suggestive developments, the link between gender and abstraction at the level of conceptual structure remains unclear.

In addition to the fact that CLT focuses on observers and not concepts, the methodological variation and modest scale of prior studies limit their ability to examine whether gender is systematically entangled with conceptual structure.

Joshi et al. 47 focus on the supply side-the abstraction of the language that men and women produce-rather than on the gendered associations that concepts themselves carry, and their finding that the gender gap closes when audience construal distance is made salient leaves open whether abstraction is male-coded in the semantics of concepts or only for the people using these concepts to particular audiences.
text.formatted: Joshi et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">47</ref> focus on the supply side-the abstraction of the language that men and women produce-rather than on the gendered associations that concepts themselves carry, and their finding that the gender gap closes when audience construal distance is made salient leaves open whether abstraction is male-coded in the semantics of concepts or only for the people using these concepts to particular audiences.

text.text: Bailey and Leshin's study 49 is an opinion piece without new empirical analyses or data; and Dodson et al.'s studies 48 rely on survey samples of a few hundred participants who describe or rate individual men and women, with a primary focus on descriptions of men and women in different occupations.
text.formatted: Bailey and Leshin's study <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">49</ref> is an opinion piece without new empirical analyses or data; and Dodson et al.'s studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">48</ref> rely on survey samples of a few hundred participants who describe or rate individual men and women, with a primary focus on descriptions of men and women in different occupations.

text.text: Altogether, it remains open whether gendered abstraction merely reflects (i) supply-side differences in how women and men speak, (ii) differences in psychological distance unrelated to concepts themselves, (iii) role dynamics shaping the representation of men and women in limited, specific contexts (e.g., the representation of occupations and biases relating to labor market sorting), (iv) a difference in the breadth and specificity of the categories 'men' and 'women', unrelated to concreteness-abstractness specifically, or (v) a far more general and fundamental gendering of how concrete and abstract concepts are represented across domains.
Another feature constraining prior work is its focus on textual data as the modality through which gender associations and concept abstractness are measured.

Yet, examining the concrete vs. abstract dimension of concepts benefits from examining more immediately embodied communication modalities, such as images, in which concepts are frequently represented through concrete, visual anchors.
Indeed, concreteness is often defined with respect to the imageability of concepts.

Decades of work in cognitive science have not only shown that human conceptual knowledge is richly multimodal, involving both symbolic and image-based representations 22, 51, 52 , but also more recent work demonstrates that images are an especially psychologically potent modality that amplifies gender stereotypes [53] [54] [55] .
text.formatted: Decades of work in cognitive science have not only shown that human conceptual knowledge is richly multimodal, involving both symbolic and image-based representations <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">22,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">51,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">52</ref> , but also more recent work demonstrates that images are an especially psychologically potent modality that amplifies gender stereotypes <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">[53]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">[54]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">[55]</ref> .

text.text: A full treatment of how gender is linked to the concreteness-abstractness dimension of concepts should therefore incorporate analyses of more directly embodied and concrete representations of concepts like images.

In this study, we address this gap by conducting a large-scale examination of the connection between gender and conceptual abstractness across the entire space of human concepts using billions of words and millions of images from the internet, as well as using behavioral response data of humans and large language models in controlled online tasks [56] [57] [58] [59] [60] [61] .
text.formatted: In this study, we address this gap by conducting a large-scale examination of the connection between gender and conceptual abstractness across the entire space of human concepts using billions of words and millions of images from the internet, as well as using behavioral response data of humans and large language models in controlled online tasks <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">[56]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">[57]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">[58]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">[59]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">[60]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">[61]</ref> .

text.text: The scale of our approachspanning conceptual domains and communication modalities -allows us to examine not only whether gender and concept abstractness are associated across semantic domains, but also to examine which aspects of concepts, e.g., their grammatical form, account for underlying patterns organizing these associations.

By examining the gender associations of the same concepts across both text and image, we are able to further test whether the male abstraction bias manifests both in how concepts are described, and also in how they are captured by the concrete, visual representation of concepts, which includes the use of concrete referents in images to metaphorically depict more abstract and difficult to perceive concepts 32, 33, 62.
text.formatted: By examining the gender associations of the same concepts across both text and image, we are able to further test whether the male abstraction bias manifests both in how concepts are described, and also in how they are captured by the concrete, visual representation of concepts, which includes the use of concrete referents in images to metaphorically depict more abstract and difficult to perceive concepts <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">32,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">33,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">62</ref>.

text.text: We begin by comparing crowdsourced concreteness judgments of the 103,428 most common concepts in English (comprising single 21 and multi-word expressions 63 ) with their corresponding gender associations (female or male), which we identified using the 'geometry of culture' method 53, 64 applied to the co-occurrence patterns among billions of words on the internet according to 12 distinct language models, spanning static embedding models and frontier generative models, both closed and open source (Supplementary Table 1; see 'Language Models' and 'Measuring Gender Associations' in Materials and Methods).

text.text: We find that increasingly abstract concepts carry increasingly male gender associations across all models, and that this pattern is stable across semantic domains according to WordNet's model of English concepts ('Identifying Semantic Domains' in Materials and Methods).

Given our ability to decompose the male abstraction bias across a large corpus of word forms, we further identify a clear underlying pattern across conceptual domains, namely that the male abstraction bias is tightly mapped onto grammatical word form: regardless of topic domain, verbs and adverbs are more abstract and more male-coded compared to nouns, suggesting that established stereotypes ascribing more agentic, action-oriented qualities to men [65] [66] [67] [68] [69] [70] [71] may go beyond role dynamics in specific contexts and may reach into the grammatical foundations of language.

text.text: Moreover, these findings are not unique to English.
Supplementary analyses show that the male abstraction bias replicates across distinct language families that vary in whether they explicitly grammaticalize gender.

We replicate our findings by analyzing extensive concreteness norms provided by native speakers of Mandarin Chinese, Persian, Dutch, and Estonian, which we map to gender associations identified using embedding models trained specifically on each language (Supplementary Sections 2 to 5, Supplementary Figs. 1 to 4 and Supplementary Tables 2 to 9).

text.text: Smaller sets of concreteness norms for five further languages point in the same direction (Supplementary Section 6, Supplementary Fig. 5 and Supplementary Table 10).

text.text: Next, we test whether this clear correlation between concept abstractness and masculine association holds beyond the textual modality by examining its presence in a large sample of online images collected for this study.
This multimodal approach is a valuable test of our theory given widespread concerns that textual representations are a limited measurement of both cultural associations and human thought 53, 72 .
text.formatted: This multimodal approach is a valuable test of our theory given widespread concerns that textual representations are a limited measurement of both cultural associations and human thought <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">53,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">72</ref> .

text.text: This is, based on the present review of the literature, the first large-scale examination of the relationship between concreteness judgments and image-based associations.

For this analysis, we collected roughly 300 Google images for each of the 40,000 concepts associated with crowdsourced human concreteness judgments in Brysbaert et al.'s study 21 , yielding 11,346,925 images.
text.formatted: For this analysis, we collected roughly 300 Google images for each of the 40,000 concepts associated with crowdsourced human concreteness judgments in Brysbaert et al.'s study <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">21</ref> , yielding 11,346,925 images.

text.text: We then applied a recent 11 billion parameter, open-source large language model (Llama-3.2-11B-Vision-Instruct) to classify all of the objects in each of the images, including the number of human faces in each image, as well as their associated gender (male or female) 73, 74 ('Image Data' and 'Image Classification' in Materials and Methods).
text.formatted: We then applied a recent 11 billion parameter, open-source large language model (Llama-3.2-11B-Vision-Instruct) to classify all of the objects in each of the images, including the number of human faces in each image, as well as their associated gender (male or female) <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">73,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">74</ref> ('Image Data' and 'Image Classification' in Materials and Methods).

text.text: Using this approach, we test whether people are more likely to appear as concrete anchors in online images for increasingly abstract concepts, and moreover, whether people are more likely to be men when functioning as concrete anchors.

The evidence shows clearly that the probability of observing people in online images increases for more abstract concepts, and -following from the established over-representation of men online 53 -men are increasingly more likely to appear in association with abstract concepts.
text.formatted: The evidence shows clearly that the probability of observing people in online images increases for more abstract concepts, and -following from the established over-representation of men online <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">53</ref> -men are increasingly more likely to appear in association with abstract concepts.

text.text: This sheds mechanistic light on a statistical driver behind the male abstraction bias: as visual representations of people skew male -and as visual representations of abstract concepts skew toward displaying people -by statistical sampling alone, abstract concepts become more associated with men.

We go further yet to reveal the ability for image analyses to provide a novel empirical test of an outstanding hypothesis in current computational work on gender stereotypes; building on Bailey and Leshin's opinion piece 49 , we present an empirical test of the hypothesis that women are represented in a more unitary manner, while men are represented with greater breadth and diversity of association; specifically, by examining whether the images associated with more male-coded concepts (according to image and textual measures of gender) are associated with a wider variety of objects (referents) compared to female-coded concepts.

text.text: Indeed, across all techniques for measuring the gender association of a concept, more abstract concepts are not only more male, but are also associated with more diverse sets of visual referents.

Given that the analyses presented above rely on large-scale observational data, an open question is whether this bias is instantiated and measurable in the response patterns of individual humans and AI agents.

We conclude by testing whether the male abstraction bias is detectable in existing experimental data collected by separate teams to examine the free associations that humans and large language models provided when given a seed concept and requested to state, with no constraint, three concepts that come to mind 60, 61 .
text.formatted: We conclude by testing whether the male abstraction bias is detectable in existing experimental data collected by separate teams to examine the free associations that humans and large language models provided when given a seed concept and requested to state, with no constraint, three concepts that come to mind <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">60,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">61</ref> .

text.text: Across both datasets, we find that humans and all the large language models involved are significantly more likely to generate male-coded (female-coded) responses when asked to free associate for more abstract (concrete) seed words, despite no explicit prompting or priming relating either to gender or to abstractness.

This suggests that the male abstraction bias is not only a statistical pattern observed in large social datasets, but is also implicitly encoded in the spreading activation of free association patterns in human and AI psychology.

The implications for the algorithmic amplification of the male abstraction bias online -in light of the increasingly male-coded discourse surrounding the framing and theorizing of AI itself -are discussed.
We began by examining the relationship between the gender association of a concept and its concreteness in text.

Concreteness was measured using human judgements, on a scale from 1 (abstract) to 5 (concrete), for the 39,953 most common words in English 21 and for a recent extension of these norms to 62,889 multiword phrases 63 ('Concreteness Norms' in Materials and Methods).
text.formatted: Concreteness was measured using human judgements, on a scale from 1 (abstract) to 5 (concrete), for the 39,953 most common words in English <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">21</ref> and for a recent extension of these norms to 62,889 multiword phrases <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">63</ref> ('Concreteness Norms' in Materials and Methods).

text.text: The gender association of each term was measured separately in each of 12 language models that vary in their architecture, training data and year of release (see 'Language Models' and 'Measuring Gender Associations' in Materials and Methods).
Figure 1a shows that terms with more masculine associations are systematically more abstract.
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_6">1a</ref> shows that terms with more masculine associations are systematically more abstract.

text.text: Across models, the correlation between the masculine association of a term and its concreteness was negative (mean r = -0.174; 95% confidence interval (CI) across models = -0.205 to -0.142; range across models = -0.233 to -0.066; t(11) = -12.03; P = 1.1 × 10 -7 ; two-tailed one-sample t-test across models), and it was negative and significant after Bonferroni correction in 12 of 12 models (n = 85,229 to 102,842 terms per model; two-tailed Pearson's correlations; Supplementary Table 11; 'Statistical Analysis of Textual Data and Robustness Tests' in Materials and Methods).
text.formatted: Across models, the correlation between the masculine association of a term and its concreteness was negative (mean r = -0.174; 95% confidence interval (CI) across models = -0.205 to -0.142; range across models = -0.233 to -0.066; t(11) = -12.03; P = 1.1 × 10 -7 ; two-tailed one-sample t-test across models), and it was negative and significant after Bonferroni correction in 12 of 12 models (n = 85,229 to 102,842 terms per model; two-tailed Pearson's correlations; Supplementary Table <ref type="table">11</ref>; 'Statistical Analysis of Textual Data and Robustness Tests' in Materials and Methods).

text.text: Averaged across models, terms in the most feminine decile had a mean concreteness of 3.42, compared with 2.83 for terms in the most masculine decile.

The male abstraction bias replicates when separately analyzing single words (mean r = -0.085; 95% CI = -0.131 to -0.039; negative in 11 of 12 models, with one small reversal) and phrases (mean r = -0.252; 95% CI = -0.295 to -0.210; negative in 12 of 12 models) (Supplementary Section 7).
These associations are robust to lexical properties that are correlated with concreteness.

Controlling for word frequency left the correlation for single words essentially unchanged (mean β = -0.091; 95% CI across models = -0.143 to -0.039), and it remained negative (i) after controlling for word frequency, length, polysemy, age of acquisition, valence, arousal, dominance and part of speech (mean β = -0.099; 95% CI = -0.143 to -0.054; t(11) = -4.90; P = 4.7 × 10 -4 ; negative in 11 of 12 models; n = 13,069 to 13,082 words per model), (ii) when the analysis was restricted to reliably rated words, within each quintile of word frequency, and (iii) after excluding person-denoting nouns, lexically gendered terms and function words (Supplementary Section 9 and Supplementary Tables 13  to 16).

text.text: As an additional robustness test, we examined whether these results hold for human judgments along a related but distinct dimension of conceptual concreteness: the Lancaster Sensorimotor Norms 75 .
text.formatted: As an additional robustness test, we examined whether these results hold for human judgments along a related but distinct dimension of conceptual concreteness: the Lancaster Sensorimotor Norms <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">75</ref> .

text.text: Whereas concreteness ratings capture whether the referent of a concept can be experienced through the senses at all, the Lancaster norms capture how strongly a concept is experienced through each of six perceptual modalities (vision, hearing, touch, taste, smell and interoception), which we averaged into a single measure of perceptual strength.

Perceptual strength is only moderately correlated with people's concreteness judgments (r = 0.32; 95% CI = 0.31 to 0.33; P < 2.2 × 10 -16 ; n = 39,706 words), providing a meaningfully distinct and complementary analysis.

text.text: Because the norms were only collected for single words, this analysis is restricted to the 39,706 words in the concreteness norms that were rated in the Lancaster norms.
Figure 1c shows that words with more masculine associations are also lower in perceptual strength.

text.text: While these robustness tests are not sufficient for arguing that the male abstraction bias is a universal pattern across languages, they are sufficient for demonstrating based on available data that the male abstraction bias is not idiosyncratic to the English language and replicates in qualitatively distinct language families that vary along key dimensions, such as whether gender is explicitly grammaticalized in the language's morphology.

The above findings provide evidence of a stable male abstraction bias across the most common words and phrases in the English language.

However, these analyses aggregate over a wide range of concepts, topics and word forms, which raises the question of whether this pattern holds across conceptual domains or is instead driven by a subset of them.
For this reason, we decomposed our results by semantic domain.

We matched each word and phrase in the concreteness norms to WordNet 82 , a canonical lexical database of English, and assigned it the semantic domain that WordNet records for its primary sense (for example, noun.food or verb.communication); words were matched on their dominant part of speech, and phrases through their own WordNet entry or, failing that, through their head noun (see 'Identifying Semantic Domains' in Materials and Methods).

To ensure that these analyses capture the gendering of concepts rather than of people, we excluded function words, lexically gendered terms (such as 'waitress') and nouns that denote persons, leaving 31,591 words in 35 domains and 56,879 phrases in 33 domains.
Within each domain, we compared the gender association of the most abstract third of terms with that of the most concrete third, averaging with equal weight across language models.
Figure 2a,b reveals a stable pattern.
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2a</ref>,b reveals a stable pattern.

text.text: For words, the most abstract third of a domain was more male-associated than its most concrete third in 33 of 35 domains (P = 3.7 × 10 -8 ; two-tailed binomial sign test; median difference across domains = 0.10 s.d.
; P < 0.05 in 15 domains; two-tailed paired t-tests across 12 models).
text.formatted: ; P < 0.05 in 15 domains; two-tailed paired t-tests across 12 models).

text.text: For phrases, this held in 32 of 33 domains (P = 7.9 × 10 -9 ; median difference = 0.40 s.d.
; P < 0.05 in 29 domains; 12 models).
text.formatted: ; P < 0.05 in 29 domains; 12 models).

text.text: In no domain, for words or phrases, was the most concrete third significantly more male-associated.

The pattern spans domains describing physical entities (for example, noun.substance: 0.07 s.d. for the abstract third versus -0.12 s.d. for the concrete third), events and states (noun.communication: 0.07 versus -0.24) and actions (verb.creation: 0.18 versus -0.21).

This suggests that our findings are not driven by particular domains, but instead reflect a system-wide bias towards associating more abstract concepts with masculine connotations, regardless of topic.

Supplementary Section 10 illustrates this pattern at the level of individual words: for three example domains (acts of communication, general adjectives and artifact nouns) and three embedding models, it plots the continuous within-domain association and highlights the individual words that anchor its two poles-for example, in the domain of acts of communication, we find crying, singing, and whisper at the female-concrete pole against justify, condone and vindicate (all explicitly related to epistemic work) at the male-abstract pole (Supplementary Fig. 6 and Supplementary Table 17).

text.text: Our analyses do, however, reveal systematic variation by word form.
Figure 2c,d locates each grammatical word form, across all domains, in terms of its mean concreteness and its mean gender association.

text.text: For words, verbs (n = 6,198) and adverbs (n = 2,622) are not only more abstract than nouns that denote entities (n = 6,524; mean concreteness of 2.91 and 2.04 versus 4.34), but also more male-associated: the mean gender association was 0.18 s.d. for verbs (95% CI across models = 0.09 to 0.26; positive in 12 of 12 models) and 0.22 s.d. for adverbs (95% CI = 0.11 to 0.32; 12 of 12 models), compared with -0.12 s.d. for entity nouns (95% CI = -0.20 to -0.03).
Relative to entity nouns, verbs were 0.29 s.d. more male-associated (95% CI = 0.16 to 0.42; P = 0.002) and adverbs 0.33 s.d.
(95% CI = 0.19 to 0.47; P = 0.001; two-tailed Wilcoxon signed-rank tests across models).
The same pattern was roughly twice as strong for phrases: verb phrases (n = 12,601; 0.39 s.d.
; 95% CI = 0.30 to 0.47) and adverb phrases (n = 2,520; 0.31 s.d.
; 95% CI = 0.21 to 0.40) were more male-associated than entity noun phrases (n = 21,234; -0.21 s.d.
; 95% CI = -0.25 to -0.17), a difference of 0.60 s.d. between verb phrases and entity noun phrases (95% CI = 0.48 to 0.71; positive in 12 of 12 models; P < 0.001).

text.text: Adjectives and nouns for events and states were also abstract, yet they were not male-associated (Fig. 2c,d), which indicates that word form shapes gender associations beyond abstractness alone.

text.text: That the most male-coded word forms are those that describe actions, and the manner in which actions are carried out, resonates with established stereotypes that ascribe agentic and more action-oriented qualities to men more than to women [36] [37] [38] 71 .

text.text: These findings suggest that gender stereotypes relating to agency may go much deeper than role dynamics (e.g., perceptions of leadership in organizations), and may connect to fundamental grammatical structure differentiating dynamic (verbs and adverbs) and more static (noun-based) concepts.  19 and 20 report these associations for the search terms whose images contained at least one face, with statistical controls.

text.text: Next, we examined whether the male abstraction bias generalizes beyond text to the visual modality, in which we examine the role of people as concrete anchors in the representation of both concrete and abstract concepts.

For each of the 39,956 terms in the single-word concreteness norms, we collected the top images returned by Google Image search (approximately 300 images per term and 12 million images in total; see 'Image Data' in Materials and Methods), which allowed us to map the features of images onto the concreteness of the concepts they depict.
We used a recent multimodal language model (Llama-3.2-11B-Vision-Instruct 73 ) to automatically detect the faces in each image and to classify their gender.

From these classifications we derived two measures for each term: the probability that one of its images depicts a person, that is, the fraction of its images in which a face was detected, and its male association, that is, the fraction of male faces among all faces detected in its images ('Image Classification' and 'Image Analyses' in Materials and Methods).
We first examined whether abstract and concrete concepts differ in their rate of depicting people in general.
Figure 3a shows that more abstract search terms are more likely to return images of people than more concrete terms.
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">3a</ref> shows that more abstract search terms are more likely to return images of people than more concrete terms.

text.text: Among the most abstract quartile of terms, 12.8% of a term's images contained a human face on average (95% CI = 12.6% to 13.0%; n = 9,722 terms), compared with 10.1% among the most concrete quartile (95% CI = 9.8% to 10.4%; n = 9,721 terms; difference = 2.7 percentage points; 95% CI = 2.4 to 3.1; Welch's t = 14.65; d.f.

Across all terms, the probability that an image depicts a person declined with concreteness (r = -0.09; 95% CI = -0.10 to -0.08; P < 2.2 × 10 -16 ; n = 38,885 search terms; two-tailed Pearson's correlation).
text.formatted: Across all terms, the probability that an image depicts a person declined with concreteness (r = -0.09; 95% CI = -0.10 to -0.08; P < 2.2 × 10 -16 ; n = 38,885 search terms; two-tailed Pearson's correlation).

text.text: This pattern is consistent with the long-standing argument that abstract concepts are understood through reference to concrete anchors from embodied experience 9, 24, 32, 52 ; we add to this the use of large-scale visual data to examine the role of people as concrete, embodied anchors leveraged in the representation of abstract concepts.

text.text: If human bodies are the embodied anchors of abstract concepts, this raises the question of who is more likely to appear when people are used to represent them.

Consistent with prior work revealing the over-representation of men in online images 53, 54 , our analyses identify a clear statistical bias toward displaying men when images of people appear in general.
text.formatted: Consistent with prior work revealing the over-representation of men in online images <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">53,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">54</ref> , our analyses identify a clear statistical bias toward displaying men when images of people appear in general.

text.text: Across all images from all concepts, 67.26% are male, indicating a strong and significant bias toward male representation (815,096 male versus 396,719 female; Wilson 95% CI = 67.2% to 67.4%; one-sample z = 405.0; P < 10 -300 against parity; two-tailed), and the male dominance remains far above parity when search terms rather than faces are treated as the unit of sampling (cluster-robust 95% CI = 67.1% to 67.5%; z = 156.0; P < 10 -300 ; n = 35,913 search terms with at least one face).

text.text: This points toward a simple and consequential statistical mechanism leading toward the over-representation of men as concrete anchors in visual depictions of abstract concepts.

As visual representations of people skew male -and as visual representations of abstract concepts skew toward displaying people -it follows that by statistical bias alone, it is expected that abstract concepts will be more associated with men.
Indeed, Fig. 3b,c shows that, when people are depicted, they are disproportionately men, and increasingly so for more abstract concepts.

text.text: We next combined our text and image data to provide an empirical test of a recent hypothesis by Bailey and Leshin 49 , namely that people think of men as many things and of women as one: men are conceptualized in varied and wide-ranging ways, whereas women are conceptualized in a more unitary way.
text.formatted: We next combined our text and image data to provide an empirical test of a recent hypothesis by Bailey and Leshin <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">49</ref> , namely that people think of men as many things and of women as one: men are conceptualized in varied and wide-ranging ways, whereas women are conceptualized in a more unitary way.

text.text: If the male abstraction bias is connected to this asymmetry, then concepts that are more abstract, and concepts that are more male-typed, should be depicted through a wider range of visual content.

To test this, we used Llama-3.2-11B-Vision-Instruct to classify the full set of objects that appear in each image, and we counted the number of unique objects detected across the images associated with each term.

Because the number of unique objects grows with the number of images examined, and the number of images retrieved varied across terms (median = 265; mean = 256; s.d. = 39), all estimates in Fig. 4 control for the number of images in each term's image set: we regressed the number of unique objects on each predictor together with the log-transformed number of images, and we report the partial correlation and slope for the predictor, with each term's count adjusted to the mean number of images in the figure (Supplementary Section 13).

text.text: Figure 4a shows that more abstract concepts are depicted through a substantially wider range of objects (partial r = -0.44; 95% CI = -0.45 to -0.43; P < 2.2 × 10 -16 ; partial Spearman's ρ = -0.41; n = 36,124 search terms), such that each one-point decrease in concreteness corresponds to 85.8 additional unique objects at a given number of images.

text.text: More male-typed concepts, which are more abstract, are likewise depicted through a wider range of objects.

This holds when the male association of a term is measured using its images (Fig. 4b; partial r = 0.10; 95% CI = 0.09 to 0.11; P < 2.2 × 10 -16 ; ρ = 0.07; n = 35,603 search terms with at least one face) and when it is measured using its gender association in text (Fig. 4c; partial r = 0.09; 95% CI = 0.08 to 0.10; P < 2.2 × 10 -16 ; ρ = 0.10; n = 36,124 search terms; two-tailed partial Pearson's correlations controlling for the log-transformed number of images).

text.text: Importantly, recent work shows that the representation of people in online images has measurable effects on strengthening gender biases in people's representation of concepts 53, 55 .
text.formatted: Importantly, recent work shows that the representation of people in online images has measurable effects on strengthening gender biases in people's representation of concepts <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">53,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">55</ref> .

text.text: We thus proceed to test whether the male abstraction bias is indeed measurable in people's implicit associations with a wide variety of concepts.
So far, all of our findings rely on aggregate patterns in large observational datasets.
This raises the question of whether the male abstraction bias is merely an emergent statistical regularity of cultural data, or whether it is also an implicit bias in the minds of individuals.
Asking this question amounts to an out-of-sample test of whether patterns discovered in large-scale cultural data yield insights into individual cognition.
This applies as well to AI agents, which are trained on this large-scale cultural data, suggesting the ability for biases therein to propagate through the AI and its responses.

To this end, we analyzed existing data on the free associations that both humans and AI agents generate in response to a wide range of cue words: the Small World of Words dataset (SWOW) 60 , in which human participants listed the first three words that came to mind for each of more than 12,000 cues, and the LLM World of Words dataset (LWOW) 61 , which administered the same task to three large language models (Llama 3, Claude 3.5 Haiku and Mistral) alongside the human responses.
text.formatted: To this end, we analyzed existing data on the free associations that both humans and AI agents generate in response to a wide range of cue words: the Small World of Words dataset (SWOW) <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">60</ref> , in which human participants listed the first three words that came to mind for each of more than 12,000 cues, and the LLM World of Words dataset (LWOW) <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">61</ref> , which administered the same task to three large language models (Llama 3, Claude 3.5 Haiku and Mistral) alongside the human responses.

text.text: These datasets were collected by different teams for different purposes, with neither concreteness nor gender in mind, and thus provide a conservative test.

We matched each cue word to its human-rated concreteness, and we measured the gender association of every freely associated word using each of our 12 language models, which yielded the mean gender association of the responses to each cue ('Free Association Data' in Materials and Methods).
Figure 5 shows that the more concrete (abstract) a cue word is, the more feminine (masculine) the associations that humans and AI agents generate.
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">5</ref> shows that the more concrete (abstract) a cue word is, the more feminine (masculine) the associations that humans and AI agents generate.

text.text: For example, when the gender association of responses is measured using OpenAI's embedding model, the correlation between cue concreteness and response gender was r = -0.21 for humans in SWOW (95% CI = -0.22 to -0.19; n = 11,179 cues) and r = -0.21 for humans in LWOW (95% CI = -0.22 to -0.19; n = 10,495), and r = -0.35 for Llama 3 (95% CI = -0.36 to -0.33; n = 10,496), r = -0.28 for Claude 3.5 Haiku (95% CI = -0.30 to -0.27; n = 10,527) and r = -0.22 for Mistral (95% CI = -0.24 to -0.20; n = 10,527; all P < 2.2 × 10 -16 ; two-tailed Pearson's correlations).

text.text: These results are robust to the method used to measure the gender association of responses.

Averaging across all 12 scoring models, the mean correlation was -0.18 for humans in SWOW (95% CI across models = -0.25 to -0.11; t(11) = -5.73; P = 1.3 × 10 -4 ), -0.18 for humans in LWOW (-0.25 to -0.11; t(11) = -5.68; P = 1.4 × 10 -4 ), -0.22 for Llama 3 (-0.30 to -0.14; t(11) = -6.34; P = 5.5 × 10 -5 ), -0.18 for Claude 3.5 Haiku (-0.25 to -0.12; t(11) = -6.17; P = 7.0 × 10 -5 ) and -0.14 for Mistral (-0.21 to -0.08; t(11) = -4.97; P = 4.2 × 10 -4 ; two-tailed one-sample t-tests across models).

Of the 60 correlations examined, 51 were negative and significant after Bonferroni correction, six were not significant, and three were significantly positive; the latter all involved a single scoring model (ConceptNet) applied to the responses of AI agents (r ≤ 0.10).

One possible reason that ConceptNet deviates from the other models is that it is distinctly designed to factor in expert-coded taxonomic knowledge about the relationships among concepts that are not learned via population-level word association patterns.
Overall, 9 of the 12 scoring models yielded a significant negative correlation for every source of responses (Fig. 5).

text.text: These findings provide evidence that both humans and AI agents have internalized the male abstraction bias at an implicit level, as indicated by their patterns of free association.
Across the space of everyday concepts, more abstract terms and phrases are more strongly associated with men and more concrete analogs with women.

This pattern appears whether abstractness is judged by people or by AI, whether it is measured as rated concreteness or as sensorimotor strength, and whether gender is measured in the distributional structure of billions of words, in the faces that populate millions of online images, or in the free associations that humans and large language models produce in controlled online tasks.

Prior work has located gender differences in abstraction in how women and men communicate and construe events 47, 48 , or in how perceivers categorize them in different social roles 49, 50 , based consistently in modest-scale and context-specific observations (e.g., occupations in the workplace).
text.formatted: Prior work has located gender differences in abstraction in how women and men communicate and construe events <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">47,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">48</ref> , or in how perceivers categorize them in different social roles <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">49,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">50</ref> , based consistently in modest-scale and context-specific observations (e.g., occupations in the workplace).

text.text: Our results shift the level of analysis to a much broader scope: the male abstraction bias pervades conceptual structure not just as a bias for differentially describing men and women, but as a bias that warps the meanings of most conceptual domains including everyday objects and events.

Moreover, we show that the male abstraction bias maps tightly onto grammatical structure: within and across a wide variety of domains, action-oriented terms-verbs and adverbs-are both more abstract and more male-coded, whereas object-oriented nouns are more concrete and more female-coded, suggesting as a broader pattern that men are afforded dynamic representations as verbs whereas women are represented more statically and passively as nouns.

As a theoretical advance, this suggests that gender stereotypes relating to agency are not simply a macro bias that emerges in descriptions of men and women across different social roles and activities (e.g., relating to norms of leadership in the workplace); instead, they appear to be woven into the function of some of the most basic and central concepts organizing grammar.

This suggests that interventions relating to changing role dynamics among women and men (e.g., by promoting women to leadership positions), while undoubtedly important and impactful 44 , need to be complemented with broader cultural shifts relating not just to the conceptualization of people, but also to basic, systemic patterns in the representation of concepts across topic domains.
text.formatted: This suggests that interventions relating to changing role dynamics among women and men (e.g., by promoting women to leadership positions), while undoubtedly important and impactful <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">44</ref> , need to be complemented with broader cultural shifts relating not just to the conceptualization of people, but also to basic, systemic patterns in the representation of concepts across topic domains.

text.text: Generally, by showing how the male abstraction bias pervades the cultural record in both online textual and image data, this raises concern for how this bias is poised to be inherited and reproduced by any AI system trained on that record.

The free-association results indicate that this male abstraction bias is not merely an aggregate regularity of corpora but is verifiably internalized in implicit concept activation patterns that individuals reproduce without any explicit gender prime, a pattern that AI models reproduce as strongly as people do.

This reveals how the male abstraction bias is vulnerable to algorithmic amplification via a cultural evolutionary process: through AI systems, stereotypes increasingly shape decisions and judgments about what is real, and thereby become real in their consequences 55, 83 .
text.formatted: This reveals how the male abstraction bias is vulnerable to algorithmic amplification via a cultural evolutionary process: through AI systems, stereotypes increasingly shape decisions and judgments about what is real, and thereby become real in their consequences <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">55,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b83">83</ref> .

text.text: Indeed, the male abstraction bias is already visible in consequential settings.

In more than half a million LinkedIn recommendations spanning industries and occupations, men are more likely to be recommended in abstract terms and women in concrete ones 48 , and exposure to gender-biased online representations measurably shifts people's beliefs and hiring preferences, which search and generative algorithms then learn and reproduce [53] [54] [55].
text.formatted: In more than half a million LinkedIn recommendations spanning industries and occupations, men are more likely to be recommended in abstract terms and women in concrete ones <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">48</ref> , and exposure to gender-biased online representations measurably shifts people's beliefs and hiring preferences, which search and generative algorithms then learn and reproduce <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">[53]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">[54]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">[55]</ref>.

text.text: These findings also provide mechanistic insights that establish a link between literatures in cognitive science and sociology that are rarely brought together.
A key premise of embodied cognition is that humans leverage concrete referents in bodily, perceptual experience to help ground and metaphorically represent less perceivable, abstract concepts.

Our findings indicate that people play an outsized role as concrete referents for representing abstract concepts, raising the question of which kinds of people are central as concrete anchors throughout conceptual systems 32, 52, 62, [84] [85] [86] .
text.formatted: Our findings indicate that people play an outsized role as concrete referents for representing abstract concepts, raising the question of which kinds of people are central as concrete anchors throughout conceptual systems <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">32,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">52,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">62,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b84">[84]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b85">[85]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b86">[86]</ref> .

text.text: Our evidence indicates a bias toward male representation when people are used as concrete anchors in abstraction; our image data shows not only that abstract concepts are more likely to be depicted by people, but also in particular by men.
This association is shaped by systemic inequalities in human cultural evolution.

Historically, men have been privileged in their ability to cultivate abstract reasoning and to specialize in the high-status knowledge work of science, art, technology and politics, and the association of reason with masculinity is a long-standing cultural construction [87] [88] [89] [90] .
text.formatted: Historically, men have been privileged in their ability to cultivate abstract reasoning and to specialize in the high-status knowledge work of science, art, technology and politics, and the association of reason with masculinity is a long-standing cultural construction <ref type="bibr" target="#b87">[87]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b88">[88]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b89">[89]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b90">[90]</ref> .

text.text: This has given men unequal opportunity to gain recognition as symbols and role models in domains of abstract reasoning and prestigious knowledge work, on which many foundational cultural narratives are constructed.

If men are sociologically favored-through stereotypes, norms, and privileged access to cultivation and resources-to accumulate experience and symbolic recognition in abstract reasoning, then that experience may reinforce the associative bias that licenses it via a self-fulfilling prophecy 91 .
text.formatted: If men are sociologically favored-through stereotypes, norms, and privileged access to cultivation and resources-to accumulate experience and symbolic recognition in abstract reasoning, then that experience may reinforce the associative bias that licenses it via a self-fulfilling prophecy <ref type="bibr" target="#b91">91</ref> .

text.text: As this bias becomes widespread and amplified via AI, it may further entrench the conceptual strategies (e.g., the use of embodied concrete anchors for representing abstraction) that warp the foundations of cognition along gender lines.

As a theoretical advance, our findings help identify an explanatory framework in which many distinct gender stereotypes are manifestations and context-specific expressions of a simpler, more systematic associative bias running through the entire conceptual system.

Many stereotypes cast women as communal and warm-concrete, embodied qualities-and men as competent, rational, task-oriented and "colder" [36] [37] [38] 92, 93 ; note, as well, that emotions themselves are often framed as "hot" cognition, in contrast to, in Lakoff's words, "more than cool reason" 94 .
text.formatted: Many stereotypes cast women as communal and warm-concrete, embodied qualities-and men as competent, rational, task-oriented and "colder" <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">[36]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">[37]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">[38]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b92">92,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b93">93</ref> ; note, as well, that emotions themselves are often framed as "hot" cognition, in contrast to, in Lakoff's words, "more than cool reason" <ref type="bibr" target="#b94">94</ref> .

text.text: In general, men are assumed to be better at mathematics and STEM despite no empirical basis for the belief 12, [40] [41] [42] , with consequences for self-sorting into degree programs and occupations 95 .
text.formatted: In general, men are assumed to be better at mathematics and STEM despite no empirical basis for the belief <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">12,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">[40]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">[41]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">[42]</ref> , with consequences for self-sorting into degree programs and occupations <ref type="bibr" target="#b95">95</ref> .

text.text: Each of these stereotype patterns may, in fact, be a subset or extension of a deeper, more systematic semantic association between men and abstraction that pervades human thinking.

Such an association may have played a key role in the development of belief systems early in human cultural evolution, given the nearuniform association between men and the leading philosophers, scientists, political leaders and religious thinkers who set the abstract paradigms that have shaped human thought for millennia and continue to shape it today 87, 88, 96.
text.formatted: Such an association may have played a key role in the development of belief systems early in human cultural evolution, given the nearuniform association between men and the leading philosophers, scientists, political leaders and religious thinkers who set the abstract paradigms that have shaped human thought for millennia and continue to shape it today <ref type="bibr" target="#b87">87,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b88">88,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b96">96</ref>.

text.text: For broader context on the implications of our findings, it is useful to consider how AI itself is gendered.
AI understood as a highly abstract and rationally engineered model of intelligence appears to be male-coded.

News imagery about AI is dominated by male faces 97 , people attribute a male gender to chatbots and to ChatGPT when no gender cue is given 98, 99 , and the thinking machine and its makers have long been culturally coded as masculine [100] [101] [102] , with a parallel argument made for its coding as white 103 .
text.formatted: News imagery about AI is dominated by male faces <ref type="bibr" target="#b97">97</ref> , people attribute a male gender to chatbots and to ChatGPT when no gender cue is given <ref type="bibr" target="#b98">98,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b99">99</ref> , and the thinking machine and its makers have long been culturally coded as masculine <ref type="bibr" target="#b100">[100]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b101">[101]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b102">[102]</ref> , with a parallel argument made for its coding as white <ref type="bibr" target="#b103">103</ref> .

text.text: However, commercial voice assistants such as Siri, Alexa and Cortana were launched with female voices and names by default in most markets, and most text-based chatbots are designed with female names and avatars 104, 105 , a pattern feminist scholars have read as the automation of feminized service and domestic labor 106, 107 .
text.formatted: However, commercial voice assistants such as Siri, Alexa and Cortana were launched with female voices and names by default in most markets, and most text-based chatbots are designed with female names and avatars <ref type="bibr" target="#b104">104,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b105">105</ref> , a pattern feminist scholars have read as the automation of feminized service and domestic labor <ref type="bibr" target="#b106">106,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b107">107</ref> .

text.text: Experimental work also finds that bots labeled female are judged more human than those labeled male 108 , and that people exploit female-labeled AI partners more than female-labeled human ones 109 .
text.formatted: Experimental work also finds that bots labeled female are judged more human than those labeled male <ref type="bibr" target="#b108">108</ref> , and that people exploit female-labeled AI partners more than female-labeled human ones <ref type="bibr" target="#b109">109</ref> .

text.text: Wong and Kim 99 find that the default perception of ChatGPT as male reverses when its capacity to provide emotional support is made salient, and Han et al. 98 find that the male default weakens to roughly neutral when a chatbot is placed in a nursing role, which suggests AI is read as male when framed as competence and reasoning, and as female when framed as emotional care and service.
text.formatted: Wong and Kim <ref type="bibr" target="#b99">99</ref> find that the default perception of ChatGPT as male reverses when its capacity to provide emotional support is made salient, and Han et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b98">98</ref> find that the male default weakens to roughly neutral when a chatbot is placed in a nursing role, which suggests AI is read as male when framed as competence and reasoning, and as female when framed as emotional care and service.

text.text: This division sits closely alongside the gender-abstraction association we document.

As AI becomes symbolic of what people believe "superior" intelligence looks like, it may reinforce the perception that intelligence is intrinsically a form of abstract and rationalized reasoning, and that by being so it is also implicitly male, while the assistive and relational work done by the same systems continues to be coded as female.
Both tendencies arguably reinforce systemic gender inequalities.
We conclude by highlighting important limitations of our study and thus valuable directions for future research.
Our evidence is correlational and cannot by itself establish the direction of causation between gendered experience and conceptual structure.

Our aim in this study is to provide a comprehensive identification of the male abstraction bias spanning common concepts and communication modalities (online text and images), and to demonstrate the robustness of this pattern to a myriad of measurement techniques and controls.

To ensure our findings are of psychological relevance at the individual level, and are not merely a statistical pattern that emerges in large-scale social data, we successfully conducted out-of-sample tests using existing experimental data to show that the male abstraction bias is measurable in the free associations generated by humans and AI.
This provides a foundation for future research aimed at providing controlled experimental evidence of the male abstraction bias and its consequences for various psychological processes.

Moreover, while we conducted a number of robustness tests demonstrating the replicability of the male abstraction bias across nine languages from different linguistic families (which vary in whether gender is morphologically grammaticalized), nevertheless, our largest and most comprehensive analyses are from English.

Because English is the lingua franca of the internet, findings from English are the most likely to capture patterns of content association and consumption that characterize internet activity around the globe, but there remains substantial cultural variation in gender norms and concept representation that cannot be captured from these analyses.

Our cross-linguistic analyses are sufficient for demonstrating that the male abstraction bias generalizes beyond English, but identifying the extent of this generalization is a compelling direction for future studies 58, 110, 111 .
text.formatted: Our cross-linguistic analyses are sufficient for demonstrating that the male abstraction bias generalizes beyond English, but identifying the extent of this generalization is a compelling direction for future studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">58,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b110">110,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b111">111</ref> .

text.text: Given that men have occupied positions of privilege in the pursuit and dissemination of high-status, abstract knowledge work across cultures and throughout recorded history 10, 87, 89 , we expect the male abstraction bias to hold across cultures; discovering deviations from this pattern and linking such deviations to variation in conceptual, linguistic, and social structure, marks rich new terrain for computational studies of gender stereotypes and cultural evolution more broadly.

text.text: Concreteness Norms.

Human judgements of concreteness were taken from the norms of Brysbaert et al. 21 , in which crowdsourced raters evaluated 39,953 generally known English words on a scale from 1 (abstract) to 5 (concrete), and from their extension by Muraki et al. 63 to 62,889 multiword expressions, collected with the same instructions and scale.
text.formatted: Human judgements of concreteness were taken from the norms of Brysbaert et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">21</ref> , in which crowdsourced raters evaluated 39,953 generally known English words on a scale from 1 (abstract) to 5 (concrete), and from their extension by Muraki et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">63</ref> to 62,889 multiword expressions, collected with the same instructions and scale.

text.text: GPT-generated concreteness ratings for the multiword expressions (n = 62,890; Fig. 1b) were taken from Martinez et al. 28 .

text.text: Perceptual strength was taken from the Lancaster Sensorimotor Norms 75 , which rate how strongly each word's referent is experienced through each of six perceptual modalities (0-5); we averaged the six ratings for the 39,706 words that also appear in the concreteness norms and extended the measure to phrases by averaging over each phrase's constituent words (Supplementary Section 8).
