text.text: Language Models.

Gender associations were measured in 12 language models that differ in architecture, training data and year of release (Supplementary Table 1; Supplementary Section 1.3): four fixed-vocabulary static word-embedding models (word2vec, FastText, Wikipedia GloVe and ConceptNet Numberbatch); four transformer language models used without a sentence-embedding head (BERT, distilBERT, RoBERTa and GPT2); three open-weight sentence-embedding models (MPNet, Qwen3 Embedding and Nomic Embed v2); and one closed, provider-managed embedding model (OpenAI's text-embedding-3-large, labelled GPT4).
text.formatted: Gender associations were measured in 12 language models that differ in architecture, training data and year of release (Supplementary Table <ref type="table">1</ref>; Supplementary Section 1.3): four fixed-vocabulary static word-embedding models (word2vec, FastText, Wikipedia GloVe and ConceptNet Numberbatch); four transformer language models used without a sentence-embedding head (BERT, distilBERT, RoBERTa and GPT2); three open-weight sentence-embedding models (MPNet, Qwen3 Embedding and Nomic Embed v2); and one closed, provider-managed embedding model (OpenAI's text-embedding-3-large, labelled GPT4).

text.text: Each term is embedded as a complete string; the static models are queried for the phrase itself and otherwise fall back to the mean of the available token vectors.
Eight of the models cover the whole vocabulary (or all but ten terms) and the four static models cover between 87,678 and 97,051 terms.
The same 12 models are used wherever a text-based gender association appears in the paper (Figs. 1, 2, 4c and 5).
text.formatted: The same 12 models are used wherever a text-based gender association appears in the paper (Figs. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_6">1</ref>, <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2</ref>, <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">4c</ref> and <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">5</ref>).

text.text: We used the geometry-of-culture method 64 , as applied to gender in our prior work 53, 55 , which represents gender association as a position along a dimension identified via contrasting poles in embedding space.
text.formatted: We used the geometry-of-culture method <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">64</ref> , as applied to gender in our prior work <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">53,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">55</ref> , which represents gender association as a position along a dimension identified via contrasting poles in embedding space.

text.text: In each model, a gender axis was built from five seed pairs (man/woman, him/her, he/she, male/female and boy/girl): each seed term was embedded and normalised to unit length, the male-minus-female difference was averaged across the five pairs, and the mean difference was normalised (Supplementary Section 1.2, Eq.

The gender association of a term is the cosine similarity between its unit-normalised embedding and this axis, with positive values indicating masculine associations; the zero point is fixed by the seed terms rather than by the mean of the vocabulary.
Scores were computed for 103,428 terms (39,953 words and 63,475 multiword expressions) in each model.

Because the models differ in scale, gender associations are compared within models: deciles (Fig. 1) were computed separately within each model, and where gender associations are combined across models (Figs. 2 and 4c) they were first z-scored within each model and then averaged with equal weight, with confidence intervals computed across models.
text.formatted: Because the models differ in scale, gender associations are compared within models: deciles (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>) were computed separately within each model, and where gender associations are combined across models (Figs. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2</ref> and <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">4c</ref>) they were first z-scored within each model and then averaged with equal weight, with confidence intervals computed across models.

text.text: Our prior work validated this measure against human judgements of the gender associations of the same terms and showed that it is robust to the choice of seed pairs 53, 55 ; seed-pair sensitivity analyses for the cross-language replications are reported in Supplementary Tables 3, 5, 7 and 9.

text.text: To decompose the results by semantic domain (Fig. 2), each word and phrase was matched to WordNet 82 and assigned the domain that WordNet records for its primary sense (for example noun.food or verb.communication).

text.text: Words were matched within their dominant part of speech as recorded in the concreteness norms, which prevents nouns from entering verb domains through rare verb senses; phrases were matched through their own WordNet entry or, failing that, through their head noun.

Function words, lexically gendered terms (for example 'waitress') and nouns that denote persons were excluded, so that the analysis captures the gendering of concepts rather than of people, leaving 31,591 words in 35 domains and 56,879 phrases in 33 domains.
Word forms (Fig. 2c,d) follow the same mapping, with noun domains divided into those denoting events and states and those denoting entities.

text.text: Image Data.
For each of the 39,956 terms in the single-word concreteness norms 21 , we searched Google Images and retained the top results, up to 300 images per term (median 265), yielding 11,346,925 images.
text.formatted: For each of the 39,956 terms in the single-word concreteness norms <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">21</ref> , we searched Google Images and retained the top results, up to 300 images per term (median 265), yielding 11,346,925 images.

text.text: Images were downloaded into one directory per search term and named by the MD5 hash of their contents, so that byte-identical duplicates within a term collapse to a single file (Supplementary Section 1.1).

Every image was classified by Llama-3.2-11B-Vision-Instruct 73, 74 , an openweight vision-language model, run on Stanford's high-performance computing infrastructure behind an OpenAI-compatible inference endpoint.
text.formatted: Every image was classified by Llama-3.2-11B-Vision-Instruct <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">73,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">74</ref> , an openweight vision-language model, run on Stanford's high-performance computing infrastructure behind an OpenAI-compatible inference endpoint.

text.text: The model was prompted with a single fixed instruction, identical for every image and containing no reference to the search term, so that classification is conditioned on the image alone.

From its responses we obtained, for each image, a free-text list of the objects depicted, the number of human faces, and the gender (male or female) of each face together with the model's confidence in that classification.

Object labels are open-vocabulary rather than drawn from a fixed taxonomy; they were lowercased, stripped of formatting, digits and punctuation, and matched to the lexicon of the concreteness norms, and labels identical to the search term were discarded.

This yields 9,977,592 images with at least one lexicon-matched object across 39,918 search terms, and 1,211,815 detected faces (67.3% classified as male) across the 35,913 terms whose images contained at least one face.

text.text: Free Association Data.
We analysed two existing free-association datasets collected by other teams for purposes unrelated to gender or concreteness.

The Small World of Words English norms (SWOW) 60 were collected by continued free association: each participant was shown a cue word and typed the first three words that came to mind, in order, with roughly 100 participants per cue and more than 12,000 cues; we used the released strength file, which aggregates the three response slots into cue-response counts.
text.formatted: The Small World of Words English norms (SWOW) <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">60</ref> were collected by continued free association: each participant was shown a cue word and typed the first three words that came to mind, in order, with roughly 100 participants per cue and more than 12,000 cues; we used the released strength file, which aggregates the three response slots into cue-response counts.

text.text: The LLM World of Words (LWOW) 61 administered the same task to three large language models-Mistral (mistral-7b), Llama 3 (llama3.1-8b) and Claude 3.5 Haiku (claude-3-5-haiku-latest)-alongside human responses to the same cues: each model was given a cue and instructed to write the first three words it associates with it, separated by commas, and the prompt was repeated 100 times per cue, yielding three response slots per repetition, which we aggregated into cue-response counts.

text.text: In both datasets, cues and responses were lowercased and trimmed, non-responses and responses identical to the cue were removed, and cues were retained where a human concreteness rating 21 was available, leaving 11,179 SWOW cues and 10,495 to 10,527 LWOW cues per source of responses (Supplementary Section 1.4).

text.text: For each cue and each of the 12 language models, the gender association of the responses is the mean gender association of the responded words, weighted by how often each response was produced; it was correlated with the cue's concreteness using two-tailed Pearson's correlations, giving 60 correlations (five sources of responses × 12 scoring models) that were Bonferroni-corrected and summarized across scoring models as above.

The Male Abstraction Bias in Internet Culture and Large Language Models 1 Data and methods

Our lexicon is the concreteness norms of Brysbaert et al. 21 , which contain 39,954 entries covering generally known English words together with a set of two-word expressions, each rated on a five-point scale from abstract to concrete.

text.text: We searched Google Images for every term and retained up to 300 images per term.
Images were downloaded in advance into one directory per search term, each file named by the MD5 hash of its contents, so that byte-identical duplicates within a term collapse to a single file.

Each image was then labelled by Llama-3.2-11B-Vision-Instruct 73, 74 , an open-weight visionlanguage model built on the LLaMA family, run on university high-performance computing in collaboration with the DARC team.

text.text: The model was served behind an OpenAI-compatible inference endpoint and prompted with a single fixed instruction, identical for every image and containing no reference to the search term, so that labelling is conditioned on the image alone.
The prompt was 41 tokens on every call.
The model returns a short comma-separated list of the objects it identifies, in free text, so labelling is generative and open-vocabulary rather than detection against a fixed taxonomy.
This produced 11,346,925 labelled images across 39,929 search terms.
Labels were parsed from the model's response and normalised: lowercased, stripped of bullet formatting, digits and punctuation, and collapsed to single spacing.

Multiword expressions appearing in the concreteness norms were joined into single labels, labels identical to the search query were removed, and the remainder were retained where they matched the lexicon.
After parsing and lexical filtering the analysis set retains 9,977,592 images across 39,918 search terms, with a median of 265 images per term and a mean of 250.
Labels were aggregated across all images for a search term and saved to disk in two forms: a dictionary mapping each label to its occurrence count, and the list of distinct labels.
Repeated labels within an image are counted rather than collapsed, so an object token is a label occurrence.
No frequency threshold was applied at aggregation.
The dataset contains 77,170,514 object tokens across 63,540 distinct object categories, with a mean of 7.73 objects per image and a median of 5.
Every one of the 39,918 search terms has at least one recorded object.
Per term, the median is 1,952 object tokens and 800 distinct categories.
We follow the geometric approach of Kozlowski et al. 64 , applied to images and text in Guilbeault et al. 53 , which represents a cultural dimension as a direction in embedding space.
text.formatted: We follow the geometric approach of Kozlowski et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">64</ref> , applied to images and text in Guilbeault et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">53</ref> , which represents a cultural dimension as a direction in embedding space.

text.text: The gender axis is built from five seed pairs: man/woman, him/her, he/she, male/female, and boy/girl.

Each seed term is embedded and its vector normalised to unit length, the male-minus-female difference is averaged across the five pairs, and that mean difference is itself normalised to give the axis: (S1) A term's gender score is the cosine similarity between its unit-normalised embedding and this axis, g(t) = unit(⃗ v t ) ⊤ ⃗ a, so a positive score falls on the male side.
The zero point is fixed by the anchors and is independent of the mean of any corpus.

Scores were generated for 103,428 terms: 39,953 from the concreteness norms above and a further 63,475 multiword expressions from Muraki et al. 63 , deduplicated case-insensitively with the first source taking precedence.

text.text: Gender at the object level, for a given search term, is the token-weighted mean of the gender scores of its labels, where c o is the occurrence count of label o and S is the set of labels with a finite score under the model in question.
Labels without a score are excluded from both numerator and denominator.
The measure is weighted by occurrence, not computed over distinct labels.

text.text: Four fixed-vocabulary word-embedding models-word2vec-google-news-300, fasttextwiki-news-subwords-300, 300-dimensional GloVe vectors trained on Wikipedia and Gigaword ('Wikipedia GloVe') and ConceptNet Numberbatch-are queried for the exact phrase first, then for lowercase and underscore variants, and otherwise fall back to the mean of the available token vectors.
OpenAI's text-embedding-3-large ('GPT4') is called through the API and returns a 3,072-dimensional embedding of the complete string.

Three sentence-transformer models use their own native pooling: all-mpnet-base-v2 ('MPNet'), Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B ('Qwen3') and nomic-embed-text-v2-moe ('Nomic v2 MoE'); Nomic is given the prefix search_document: on both anchors and vocabulary items, as its model card requires.

Four transformer language models are used without a sentence-embedding head: gpt2 as a static embedding table, in which a term is tokenised and its vector is the mean of the input embeddings of its subword tokens, with special and padding tokens excluded; and bert-base-uncased, distilbert-base-uncased and roberta-base.

Eight of the 12 models cover the full vocabulary of 103,429 distinct terms (the three BERTfamily models all terms, and text-embedding-3-large, MPNet, Qwen3, Nomic and GPT2 all but ten); the fixed-vocabulary models cover fewer, the shortfall arising from terms absent from their vocabularies (Supplementary Table 1).

Cues and responses are lower-cased and trimmed; non-response strings (no more responses, unknown word, nan, none, na and the empty string) and responses identical to the cue are excluded.

text.text: Each rated word was scored as the cosine between its unit-normalised vector and the axis, positive values indicating masculine associations; words absent from the vector table (8.2%) were not scored, leaving 23,758 words.

As a check on the axis that does not involve concreteness, we verified that the primary axis orders the male above the female member in all 27 gendered word pairs that were not used as seeds (for example koning/koningin, acteur/actrice, oom/tante, meneer/mevrouw).

The statistics mirror Supplementary Sections 7 and 9: two-tailed Pearson's correlations with Fisher-transformed 95% confidence intervals, Spearman's rank correlations, mean concreteness within deciles of the gender score, and ordinary least squares regressions of the z-scored gender score on z-scored concreteness with heteroskedasticity-robust (HC1) standard errors, whose coefficient is a standardized β.

Covariates were word frequency (the Zipf-scaled frequency of the wordfreq library 120 , which combines subtitle, Wikipedia and web corpora; 23,407 words have an entry), length in characters, and age of acquisition from the same norms.

We also report the association within each quintile of word frequency, after excluding words that contain a gendered morpheme or a kinship or role stem (for example -man, vrouw-, -ster, vader, koning) together with the seed words themselves, and after excluding the 5% or 10% of words with the most extreme gender scores.
Finally, we recomputed the correlation for each axis obtained by dropping one seed pair from the primary set, for each of the ten kinship and role pairs on its own, and for the pronoun pairs.

Pearson's r = -0.268 (95% CI -0.279 to -0.256) and -0.292 (-0.304 to -0.280), respectively; Supplementary Tables 2 and 3 report the robustness of these estimates.

text.text: Controlling for word frequency left the estimate unchanged (β = -0.269), controlling for length reduced it slightly (β = -0.235), and controlling for frequency, length and age of acquisition together gave β = -0.245 (-0.258 to -0.231; n = 23,398).

The correlation was negative in every quintile of word frequency (r = -0.233 to -0.304), and it was unchanged or slightly stronger after excluding words containing a gendered morpheme or kinship stem together with the seed words (r = -0.268; n = 23,062) and after excluding the 5% or 10% of words with the most extreme gender scores (r = -0.281 and -0.284), so it is not carried by a small set of explicitly gendered words.
The same holds for the extended axis in every specification (β or r between -0.221 and -0.335).

The Dutch result is, however, more sensitive to the choice of seed pairs than the English results, and Supplementary Table 3 reports this sensitivity in full, together with the five most feminine and five most masculine words under each axis.

text.text: Every axis built from several unambiguous kinship or role pairs is negative: the primary set (-0.268), the extended set (-0.292), each of the five axes obtained by dropping one pair from the primary set (-0.148 to -0.339), and the first principal component of the ten pair differences (-0.215), which captures 43% of their variance and on which all ten pairs load positively (0.38 to 0.84).

The feminine extreme of these axes is populated by words for girls, brides and feminine appearance (bruidsmeisje, tienermeisje, brunette, lingerie) and the masculine extreme by words for leaders and military or feudal roles (aanvoerder, voorman, bevelhebber, veldheer, leenheer), as expected of a gender axis.

Single pairs are noisier: six of the ten kinship and role pairs taken alone are negative (from heer/dame, -0.375, to opa/oma, -0.136), whereas oom/tante and mannelijk/vrouwelijk are close to zero and zoon/dochter and man/vrouw are positive (0.122 and 0.239).

The man/vrouw axis illustrates why single pairs are unreliable in a static vector table: its masculine extreme consists of colloquial terms for a foolish or idle man (prutser, malloot, mafkees, hooligan), reflecting the use of man as an informal term of address, and its feminine extreme of abstract nouns for sexuality and motherhood (moederschap, seksualiteit, zwangerschap), so that it conflates gender with register and with the concreteness of the seed words themselves.
Averaging across several pairs removes this pair-specific variance, which is the rationale for the multi-pair construction of Eq.
The pronoun pairs of the English axis cannot be used in Dutch, and including them reverses the sign (pronoun set, r = 0.217; hij/zij alone, 0.365; hem/haar alone, 0.210).

These axes are visibly not gender axes: the "feminine" extreme of the hij/zij axis is wij, we, hun, zij and gezamenlijk (we, they, their, jointly), because zij also means they, and that of the hem/haar axis is van, hun, alsook and rondom (of, their, as well as, around), because haar also means hair and is a possessive.
Seed pairs for other languages should therefore be checked for this kind of ambiguity before an axis is built, and the extremes of the resulting axis inspected, as done here.

In sum, with seed pairs that refer unambiguously to women and men, the association between masculine connotation and abstractness replicates in Dutch with a magnitude at the upper end of the English estimates, in a language whose nouns carry no grammatical gender.

Extending the test to languages with grammatical gender, and to languages further from English, requires concreteness norms of comparable scale, which currently exist at the scale of ten thousand words or more only for Estonian and Mandarin 76, 121 .

text.text: The Estonian, Chinese and Persian tests are reported in Supplementary Sections 3 to 5.
Estonian offers a second, and typologically more distant, test of the male abstraction bias.

It is a Finno-Ugric rather than an Indo-European language, and it is a genderless language: nouns, adjectives and pronouns carry no grammatical gender, and a single third-person pronoun (tema/ta) covers both he and she.

The concreteness norms of Proos and Aigro 76 provide ratings for 35,979 Estonian lemmas on a continuous scale from 0 (abstract) to 10 (concrete), collected from 2,278 native speakers; we used all of them (mean 6.39; s.d.

Gender associations were measured in fastText's Estonian word vectors 81 , which were trained on the Estonian portions of Common Crawl and Wikipedia (2 million words, 300 dimensions) and are, like the Dutch spaCy vectors, a model trained on the language itself rather than an English or multilingual model.

text.text: The 33,031 rated lemmas (91.8%) that occur in the fastText vocabulary were scored; words absent from it were not reconstructed from character n-grams.
The procedure follows the Dutch replication shown above in every respect but two.

First, because Estonian has no gendered pronouns, both seed sets consist entirely of kinship and role nouns and the adjective pair for masculine/feminine: the primary axis uses mees/naine (man/woman), poiss/tüdruk (boy/girl), mehelik/naiselik (masculine/feminine), isa/ema (father/mother) and vend/õde (brother/sister), which are the Estonian counterparts of the five pairs of the Dutch
Both axes order the male above the female member in all 20 gendered word pairs that were not used as seeds (for example peigmees/pruut, näitleja/näitlejanna, noormees/neiu, mehed/naised).

Second, word frequency was taken from the order of the fastText vocabulary, which lists words by their frequency in the training corpus, and the Estonian norms provide no age-of-acquisition ratings; in their place we use the rater standard deviation distributed with the norms to restrict the analysis to reliably rated words.

text.text: The feminine extremes of these axes are words for women, women's clothing and cosmetics (sõbranna 'female friend', õde 'sister', kleit 'dress', pulmakleit 'wedding dress', meik 'makeup', ämmaemand 'midwife') and the masculine extremes the role nouns listed above, as expected of a gender axis.

Single pairs are again noisier: seven of the ten are negative on their own (from isa/ema, -0.295, to onu/tädi, -0.052), poiss/tüdruk and kuningas/kuninganna are indistinguishable from zero, and mees/naine is positive (0.054).

The last is the same pair that reversed in Dutch (man/vrouw, 0.239) and for a parallel reason: mees is the productive compound head for male occupational nouns, so its neighbourhood consists of concrete role nouns (raudmees 'strongman', varumees 'substitute player', tsiklimees 'motorcyclist'), whereas the neighbourhood of naine is dominated by nouns of pregnancy and motherhood (emadus 'motherhood', rasedus 'pregnancy', raseduskuu 'month of pregnancy'), so that the bare pair conflates gender with the concreteness of the seed words' own derivatives.

The adjective pair mehelik/naiselik shows a further, fastText-specific weakness: because fastText represents words through character n-grams, its masculine extreme includes unrelated words that merely share the suffix string (ahelik, võimeline, liikmeline), which is why that pair contributes little to the axis (loading 0.29) and why its omission leaves the primary estimate unchanged (-0.124).
Averaging over several unambiguous pairs removes this pair-specific variance, as it did in Dutch.
In sum, the male abstraction bias replicates in a genderless Finno-Ugric language, in a second embedding family, with a magnitude between the English and Dutch estimates.

Across the two replications, the same methodological regularities appear: axes averaged over several kinship and role pairs agree in sign and are validated by held-out gendered pairs, whereas the bare man/woman pair on its own is unreliable in both languages; and the words at the masculine extreme are predominantly nouns for men in roles, whose concreteness as person nouns attenuates rather than produces the association.
Chinese provides a third test, in a non-alphabetic script and in the language with the largest number of native speakers.

Like Estonian, Mandarin Chinese has no grammatical gender: nouns and adjectives are unmarked, and the third-person pronoun is a single syllable, tā, whose written forms 他 (he) and 她 (she) were only differentiated in the twentieth century.
Two sets of human concreteness ratings for two-character words are available.

The norms of Chan and Tse 77 cover 25,281 two-character words of standard written Chinese, rated on a 7-point scale by Cantonese-speaking participants in Hong Kong; because the distributed file gives each word in both traditional and simplified characters, the 25,044 distinct simplified forms could be scored directly (mean 4.60; s.d.
The norms of Song and Li 78 cover 3,783 simplified two-character words rated on the same 7-point scale by Mainland Mandarin speakers (mean 4.77; s.d.
1.05), and serve to check that the result does not depend on the Hong Kong sample.

Gender associations were measured in the static word vectors distributed with spaCy's zh_core_web_lg model (version 3.8.0; 500,000 entries, 300 dimensions) 80 , which are fastText CBOW vectors trained on the Chinese portions of OSCAR Common Crawl and Wikipedia; 23,961 of the Chan and Tse words (95.7%) and 3,782 of the Song and Li words are in its vocabulary.
text.formatted: Gender associations were measured in the static word vectors distributed with spaCy's zh_core_web_lg model (version 3.8.0; 500,000 entries, 300 dimensions) <ref type="bibr" target="#b80">80</ref> , which are fastText CBOW vectors trained on the Chinese portions of OSCAR Common Crawl and Wikipedia; 23,961 of the Chan and Tse words (95.7%) and 3,782 of the Song and Li words are in its vocabulary.

text.text: The seed pairs are the Chinese counterparts of the Dutch and Estonian primary and extended sets: 男人/女人 (man/woman), 男孩/女孩 (boy/girl), 男性/女性 (male/female), 父亲/母亲 (father/mother) and 哥哥/姐姐 (elder brother/elder sister) for the primary axis, with 儿子/女儿
Because the written pronoun distinction is unambiguous in Chinese, unlike in Dutch, a pronoun variant that replaces 哥哥/姐姐 with 他/她 is also reported.
The primary axis orders the male above the female member in all 18 held-out gendered pairs (for example 丈夫/妻子, 新郎/新娘, 王子/公主, 皇帝/皇后), and the extended and pronoun axes in 17 of 18.

Because every item is a two-character word, length cannot vary and is not controlled; word frequency is the log corpus frequency distributed with each set of norms, and the Chan and Tse rater standard deviations define the reliably rated subset.
Words containing a gender-marking character (男, 女, 父, 母, 哥, 姐, 夫, 妻, 他, 她 and the like) are the lexically gendered terms for the exclusion check.
Supplementary Fig. 3 shows that the pattern of Fig. 1a replicates in Chinese.
text.formatted: Supplementary Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">3</ref> shows that the pattern of Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_6">1a</ref> replicates in Chinese.

text.text: Across the 23,961 Chan and Tse words, more masculine words are more abstract (r = -0.111; 95% CI = -0.123 to -0.098; P < 2.2 × 10 -16 ; Spearman's ρ = -0.101), and mean concreteness falls from 4.76 in the most feminine decile to 4.49 in the most masculine, a difference of 0.27 points on the 7-point scale or 0.38 s.d. of the ratings.
text.formatted: Across the 23,961 Chan and Tse words, more masculine words are more abstract (r = -0.111; 95% CI = -0.123 to -0.098; P < 2.2 × 10 -16 ; Spearman's ρ = -0.101), and mean concreteness falls from 4.76 in the most feminine decile to 4.49 in the most masculine, a difference of 0.27 points on the 7-point scale or 0.38 s.d. of the ratings.

text.text: The extended axis gives r = -0.193 (-0.205 to -0.181; ρ = -0.193) with a strictly monotone decline across all ten deciles, from 4.86 to 4.36 (0.68 s.d.); the pronoun axis gives r = -0.168 (-0.180 to -0.155).

In units of the ratings' standard deviation, the Chinese estimates are thus in the range of the Estonian estimates (0.37 and 0.44 s.d. for the two axes) and between the English single-word (0.28 s.d.) and Dutch (0.84 s.d.) estimates.

Supplementary Table 6 shows that the association survives the available controls and exclusions: controlling for word frequency (β = -0.112 and -0.197 for the two axes), restricting the analysis to reliably rated words (r = -0.129 and -0.200), excluding words that contain a gender-marking character together with the seed words (r = -0.095 and -0.187), and excluding the 5% or 10% of words with the most extreme gender scores (r = -0.088 and -0.082 for the primary axis; -0.184 and -0.168 for the extended axis).

text.text: Unlike in Estonian, the last exclusion weakens the primary estimate somewhat, because in Chinese it is the feminine extreme that is populated by lexically gendered words (see below).

text.text: The Mainland sample gives the same answer with larger effects.

Across the 3,782 Song and Li words, r = -0.189 (95% CI = -0.219 to -0.158) for the primary axis, -0.226 (-0.256 to -0.196) for the extended axis and -0.288 (-0.316 to -0.258) for the pronoun axis (all P < 10 -30 ); mean concreteness falls from 5.22 to 4.50 across the deciles of the primary axis (0.68 s.d.) and from 5.33 to 4.44 across those of the extended axis (0.84 s.d.), and the estimates remain between -0.121 and -0.283 after the frequency control and the three exclusions.

text.text: The male abstraction bias in written Chinese is therefore present whether the ratings come from Cantonese-speaking or Mandarin-speaking raters, and is if anything stronger in the Mainland sample.
The words at the two extremes of the Chinese axes (Supplementary Table 7) show the bias in an unusually direct form.
text.formatted: The words at the two extremes of the Chinese axes (Supplementary Table <ref type="table">7</ref>) show the bias in an unusually direct form.

text.text: The feminine extreme of the primary axis consists of words for women and for feminine appearance-少妇 'young married woman', 美女 'beautiful woman', 女人 'woman', 少女 'girl', 姐姐 'elder sister', 嫂子 'sister-in-law', 白嫩 'fair and delicate (of skin)'-whereas its masculine extreme consists not of words for men but of abstract words for chance, inference and strategy: 运气 'luck', 如何 'how', 数值 'numerical value', 设法 'to find a way', 概率 'probability', 祈 祷 'to pray', with 分析 'analysis' and 推测 'to infer' at the masculine extreme of the pronoun axis.

The extended axis, whose seeds include more kin and rank terms, adds the vocabulary of rank and command to the masculine extreme (长兄 'eldest brother', 继位 'to succeed to the throne', 带兵 'to lead troops', 功劳 'merit').

The asymmetry-women represented by words for women, men by the vocabulary of reasoning and authority-is the lexical counterpart of the pattern documented in Figs. 2 and 4, and it is the reason the exclusion of lexically gendered words lowers the Chinese estimate: the words removed lie almost entirely at the concrete, feminine end.
text.formatted: The asymmetry-women represented by words for women, men by the vocabulary of reasoning and authority-is the lexical counterpart of the pattern documented in Figs. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2</ref> and <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">4</ref>, and it is the reason the exclusion of lexically gendered words lowers the Chinese estimate: the words removed lie almost entirely at the concrete, feminine end.

text.text: Supplementary Table 7 also reports the sensitivity to the seed pairs, which repeats the pattern of the other two languages.

text.text: Every multi-pair axis is negative: the primary set (-0.111), the extended set (-0.193), the pronoun set (-0.168), each axis obtained by dropping one pair from the primary set (-0.040 to -0.168) and the first principal component of the ten pair differences (-0.191; 29% of their variance; all ten pairs loading positively, 0.30 to 0.68).
Nine of the eleven single pairs are negative on their own, from 先生/女士 (-0.332) and 他/她 (-0.266) to 爷爷/奶奶 (-0.058); 男 孩/女孩 is indistinguishable from zero; and 男性/女性 is positive (0.139).

As with man/vrouw in Dutch and mees/naine in Estonian, the reversed pair is the one whose members have a dominant non-referential use: 男性 and 女性 are the terms of medical and sexual-health discourse, and the masculine extreme of that axis is accordingly 早泄, 肾虚, 睾丸, 包皮, 阳痿 (premature ejaculation, kidney deficiency, testicle, foreskin, impotence), which are concrete.

Conversely, the strongest single pair, 先生/女士, owes part of its strength to the use of 先生 for 'teacher' or 'master', so that its masculine extreme is populated by scholarly words (先师 'late teacher', 著书 'to write books', 遗著 'posthumous works'); this pair is not in the primary set, whose estimate is the conservative one.
Averaging over several unambiguous pairs again removes these pair-specific effects.

In sum, the male abstraction bias replicates in written Chinese across two independently collected sets of human concreteness norms, two speaker populations and a logographic script, with a magnitude comparable to Estonian and, in the Mainland sample, to Dutch.

With Dutch and Estonian, the text-based result now holds in three languages from three families (Germanic, Finno-Ugric and Sinitic), two of which have no grammatical gender at all, and in each the pattern appears whenever the gender axis is built from several unambiguous kinship and role pairs; Supplementary Section 5 adds a fourth language, Persian.
The male abstraction bias in Chinese is robust to word frequency, rater reliability and the composition of the vocabulary.

Five further languages with smaller concreteness norms, and the pattern across languages

Human concreteness norms also exist, at a smaller scale, for several further languages, and the same test can be run on them with the same language-specific fastText vectors 81 and the same construction of the gender axis from five kinship and role seed pairs.

text.text: We did so for every such language whose norms are publicly redistributed and whose seed words are all present in the vectors: Italian (1,121 words; the Italian adaptation of the ANEW list 113 ), French (1,659 words 114 ), Turkish (568 words 112 ), Portuguese (3,800 words; the Minho Word Pool 115 ) and Indonesian (1,487 words 116 ).

text.text: Two caveats apply to all five.

With the exception of the Portuguese set, these word lists were assembled for affective or age-of-acquisition norming and so sample the vocabulary unevenly, with an emphasis on emotionally loaded words and words for people; and at a few hundred to a few thousand words they do not support the decile, covariate and within-domain analyses of the preceding sections.

We therefore report for each language the correlation between the gender score and concreteness with its 95% confidence interval, the same correlation for the extended ten-pair axis, the range of correlations obtained by dropping one seed pair from the primary set, and a check that the axis orders the male above the female member of ten held-out gendered word pairs (Supplementary Table 10).

text.text: The seed pairs are the counterparts of those used for the other languages (for example uomo/donna, ragazzo/ragazza, padre/madre in Italian; adam/kadın, oğlan/kız, baba/anne in Turkish; pria/wanita, ayah/ibu, saudara/saudari in Indonesian), and the axis passed the held-out check in all ten pairs in every language.

In all five languages the correlation is negative (Supplementary Table 10): Turkish (r = -0.244; 95% CI = -0.320 to -0.165), Italian (-0.187; -0.243 to -0.129), French (-0.118; -0.166 to -0.070), Portuguese (-0.039; -0.071 to -0.008; P = 0.015) and Indonesian (-0.027; -0.079 to 0.025; P = 0.31).

text.text: The words at the extremes of the axes are gendered in every language-donna, ragazza, regina, suora, madre against fratello, amico, padre, ragazzo in Italian; mère, reine, soeur, tante, dame against homme, frère, bougre in French; hamile 'pregnant', kadın 'woman', makyaj 'make-up' against dede 'grandfather', baba 'father', berber 'barber' in Turkish; mulher, rainha, freira, mãe, parteira 'midwife' against velho 'old man', irmão, pai, homem, sábio 'wise man' in Portuguese; anggun 'graceful', cantik 'beautiful', gaun 'gown', ibu, wanita against paman 'uncle', berkelahi 'to fight', ayah, abang, tampan 'handsome' in Indonesian-so that each axis is a gender axis in the sense of the preceding sections, with the feminine pole again anchored in appearance and maternity and the masculine pole in kin, age and roles.
Supplementary Fig. 5 places these five estimates alongside the four large-norm replications and the English single-word estimate of Fig. 1a.
text.formatted: Supplementary Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">5</ref> places these five estimates alongside the four large-norm replications and the English single-word estimate of Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_6">1a</ref>.

text.text: Across the nine languages other than English, the correlation is negative in all nine and its confidence interval excludes zero in eight (two-tailed binomial sign test on the direction, P = 0.0039); the median correlation is -0.124, and the English single-word mean across the 12 models (-0.085) lies in the middle of the cross-language distribution.

The estimates do not sort by the gender system of the language: the three largest are Dutch (common/neuter gender only), Turkish and Persian (genderless), and the languages with masculine/feminine grammatical gender (Italian, French, Portuguese) span the range from the fourth-largest (Italian) to the smallest significant estimate (Portuguese).

The Romance estimates are, on average, somewhat smaller than those of the genderless languages, which would be expected if the gender axis of a language with grammatical gender partly encodes the grammatical gender of nouns-a component unrelated to concreteness that adds noise to the gender score-but the present data cannot separate that explanation from differences in the norm sets, and the question is better addressed with norms that record grammatical gender directly.

In sum, the available non-English norms, large and small, give the same answer: more masculine words are rated as more abstract, in nine languages from four families (Indo-European, in its Germanic, Romance and Iranian branches; Uralic; Sino-Tibetan; and Turkic, with Austronesian inconclusive) written in three scripts, with and without grammatical gender.

text.text: We measured the perceptual strength of a word as its mean rating across the six modalities.

Fig. 1c of the main text reports the relationship between gender association and perceptual strength for the 39,706 words in the concreteness norms that were rated in the Lancaster norms (Supplementary Table 12, left).

text.text: Here we ask whether the same relationship holds for multiword phrases, which the Lancaster norms do not cover.
We extended the norms to phrases by assigning each phrase the mean perceptual strength of its constituent words that appear in the norms.
Of the 62,889 phrases in the concreteness norms, 62,321 contained at least one such word; on average 91% of a phrase's words were covered, and 80% of phrases were covered completely.

This extension rests on two simplifying assumptions: that the perceptual strength of a phrase is compositional, which does not hold for idiomatic phrases, and that function words, which are low in perceptual strength, contribute equally to the average.
Averaging also compresses the range of perceptual strength among phrases relative to words.
The extension should therefore be read as a conservative approximation.

We repeated the analysis described in Supplementary Section 7, replacing concreteness with perceptual strength, for (i) the words alone, as in Fig. 1c, (ii) the phrases alone and (iii) words and phrases pooled.

text.text: The gate is what makes the sense-based mapping safe: without it, common nouns leak into verb domains through rare verb senses (WordNet lists butterfly as a communication verb, "to talk amorously", and skirt as "to evade an issue"), even though the gender score of the word form is dominated by its nominal use.

The small set of two-word entries in the norms carries no dominant part of speech, and such entries are admitted only to noun.artifact, and only when WordNet lists them exclusively as nouns (for example, wedding dress).
This yields 1,393 words for verb.communication, 5,024 for adj.all and 4,634 for noun.artifact.

At the female-concrete pole the domains fill with garments and domestic artifacts (wedding dress, blouse, lingerie, doll, tiara), gendered descriptors of appearance (blonde, pregnant) and expressive, embodied acts of communication (crying, singing, whisper); at the male-abstract pole sit evaluative and normative terms (heinous, unforgivable, blasphemous), verbs of judgement and authority (justify, condone, vindicate, excommunicate) and abstract-rated nouns (juggernaut, mainstay, motive).

text.text: The association was negative in every specification, for both measures, and every 95% confidence interval excluded the null value (zero for β and ρ, one for odds ratios).
Its magnitude, however, depended substantially on the treatment of terms without faces.
For concreteness, the main-text association was β = -0.225 (95% CI -0.235 to -0.214).

A linear control for the number of faces changed this little (β = -0.204), because a linear term does not absorb the discontinuity at zero faces; controlling for log(1 + faces) reduced it to β = -0.074, an indicator for any face to β = -0.047, and the indicator together with log(1 + faces) and word frequency to β = -0.031 (-0.039 to -0.024).

Restricting the sample to terms with at least one face gave β = -0.070 (-0.082 to -0.059), and β = -0.048 (-0.059 to -0.037) with controls for log(1 + faces) and word frequency; estimates remained between -0.041 and -0.056 when requiring at least 5, 10 or 20 faces.

Roughly two-thirds of the main-text association with concreteness is thus attributable to terms that return no faces, and the remainder to a lower male fraction among the faces that are shown: among terms with at least one face, the mean male fraction declined from 0.670 in the most abstract bin to 0.624 in the most concrete bin.
For perceptual strength, the main-text association was β = -0.084 (-0.094 to -0.074), and β = -0.049 (-0.060 to -0.038) among terms with at least one face (β = -0.048 with controls).
In contrast to concreteness, the association strengthened as the minimum number of faces increased, to β = -0.062, -0.077 and -0.097 (-0.111 to -0.082) for at least 5, 10 and 20 faces.

The estimators that weight terms by their number of faces yielded the smallest estimates for concreteness: β = -0.015 (-0.028 to -0.002; P = 0.020) in the face-weighted regression, and an odds ratio of 0.987 per standard deviation (0.980 to 0.994; P = 1.8 × 10 -4 ) in the face-level quasi-binomial model, indicating that the association with concreteness is weaker among terms that return many faces.
The corresponding estimates for perceptual strength were β = -0.065 (-0.077 to -0.053) and an odds ratio of 0.946 (0.940 to 0.953).
Rank correlations among terms with faces were ρ = -0.047 for concreteness and ρ = -0.048 for perceptual strength.
Treating terms without faces as neutral rather than as 0% male gave β = -0.123 (-0.133 to -0.113) for concreteness and β = -0.062 (-0.072 to -0.052) for perceptual strength.

Taken together, the direction of the association shown in the main text is robust to the number of detected faces, but its magnitude is an upper bound: conditional on a term returning faces, a one-standard-deviation increase in either concreteness or perceptual strength is associated with a decrease of approximately 0.05 standard deviations in the fraction of faces that are male.
In Fig. 4 of the main text, the visual diversity of a search term is the number of unique objects detected across its Google Images.
text.formatted: In Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">4</ref> of the main text, the visual diversity of a search term is the number of unique objects detected across its Google Images.

text.text: Up to 300 images were retrieved per term, but the number available varied: among the 36,124 terms analysed, the median was 265 images (mean = 256; s.d. = 39; range = 3 to 300), and 1,583 terms (4.4%) had fewer than 200.

Because each additional image can only add to the set of distinct objects, the number of unique objects rises with the number of images (r = 0.47 with the number of images and 0.46 with its logarithm), so an association between a predictor and visual diversity could in principle arise if the predictor were correlated with the number of images retrieved.

In practice the number of images was only weakly related to the three predictors (r = 0.05 with concreteness, 0.05 with the fraction of male faces and -0.02 with the text-based gender association), but the terms with the most images (280 or more; 14% of terms) were disproportionately concrete (mean concreteness = 3.59, compared with 2.86 for the remaining terms) and yet had fewer unique objects (755 compared with 783), so the bivariate association in Fig. 4a slightly understates the association at a fixed number of images.

Specifications (3)-(5) vary the functional form of the control: the untransformed number of images, a quadratic in the number of images and fixed effects for deciles of the number of images, which make no assumption about functional form.

Specification (6) adds the log-transformed total number of object tokens detected for the term; this is a stricter control, because the number of objects detected per image is itself part of what the diversity measure captures.
Specifications ( 7) and ( 8) restrict the analysis to the 34,541 terms with at least 200 images (34,149 for panel (b)), without and with the log control.

text.text: The association between concreteness and visual diversity strengthened under every control, from r = -0.38 without the control to between -0.39 (decile fixed effects) and -0.48 (log images and object tokens), with the slope changing from 83.5 to between 55.2 and 90.0 additional unique objects per point of concreteness.

The association with the fraction of male faces was essentially unchanged by the number of images (r = 0.11 without the control; 0.10 under specifications (2)-( 5)) and remained positive and highly significant under the stricter object-token control (r = 0.06).

text.text: The association with the text-based gender association rose slightly under the image controls (r = 0.07 without the control; 0.09 under specifications (2)-(4) and 0.07 with decile fixed effects) and was larger still under the object-token control (r = 0.15).
Restricting the analysis to terms with at least 200 images gave the same picture.
Across all 24 estimates, every association retained its sign, and every P value was below 2.2 × 10 -16.

text.text: Persian provides a fourth test, in a language of the Indo-Iranian branch of Indo-European written in a right-to-left script.
Like Estonian and Chinese, Persian is genderless: nouns, adjectives and articles carry no grammatical gender, and the third-person pronoun u covers both he and she.

The concreteness norms are those of the Extrapolated Persian Lexical Affect Norms (E-PLAN) of Nemati et al. 79 , which differ from the other norms used in this paper in how they were collected: rather than rating each word on a scale, 1,071 Persian speakers judged small sets of words, choosing the most and the least concrete word in each set (best-worst scaling), and each word's score is derived from how often it was chosen as most versus least concrete and expressed on a scale from 0 (abstract) to 1 (concrete).
text.formatted: The concreteness norms are those of the Extrapolated Persian Lexical Affect Norms (E-PLAN) of Nemati et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">79</ref> , which differ from the other norms used in this paper in how they were collected: rather than rating each word on a scale, 1,071 Persian speakers judged small sets of words, choosing the most and the least concrete word in each set (best-worst scaling), and each word's score is derived from how often it was chosen as most versus least concrete and expressed on a scale from 0 (abstract) to 1 (concrete).

text.text: The human-rated set covers 2,924 words (mean 0.51; s.d.
0.13), and the authors validate it against earlier Persian rating-scale norms.

They also provide extrapolated scores for 85,716 words, obtained by fitting generalized additive models on principal components of Persian skip-gram embeddings to the human judgements (R² = 0.68 for concreteness); because these scores are themselves derived from word embeddings, we use them only as a secondary check and report the human-rated words as the result.
Gender associations were measured in fastText's Persian word vectors 81 (Common Crawl and Wikipedia; 2 million words, 300 dimensions); every one of the 2,924 human-rated words has a vector.
text.formatted: Gender associations were measured in fastText's Persian word vectors <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">81</ref> (Common Crawl and Wikipedia; 2 million words, 300 dimensions); every one of the 2,924 human-rated words has a vector.

text.text: The seed pairs are the Persian counterparts of the primary and extended sets of the other languages, all kinship and role nouns and one adjective pair, since Persian has no gendered pronouns: mard/zan (man/woman), pesar/dokhtar (boy/girl), mardāne/zanāne (masculine/feminine), pedar/mādar (father/mother) and barādar/khāhar (brother/sister) for the primary axis, with amu/amme (uncle/aunt), shāh/malake (king/queen), āqā/khānom (Mr/Ms), pedarbozorg/mādarbozorg (grandfather/grandmother) and dāmād/arus (groom/bride) added for the extended axis.
Both axes order the male above the female member in 10 of 11 held-out gendered pairs (for example mardān/zanān 'men/women', pirmard/pirzan 'old man/old woman', shāhzāde/shāhdokht 'prince/princess').

The procedure otherwise follows the Dutch replication: word frequency is the rank of the word in the fastText vocabulary (the norms carry no frequency counts or rater standard deviations), length is the number of characters, and words containing a gender-marking stem (mard, zan, pesar, dokhtar, pedar, mādar and the like) are the lexically gendered terms for the exclusion check.

text.text: Every multi-pair axis is negative, within a narrow range: the primary set (-0.194), the extended set (-0.208), each axis obtained by dropping one pair from the primary set (-0.170 to -0.188) and the first principal component of the ten pair differences (-0.211; 26% of their variance; all ten pairs loading positively, 0.24 to 0.64).

Nine of the ten single pairs are negative on their own, from dāmād/arus (-0.299) to barādar/khāhar (-0.093); unlike in Dutch, Estonian and Chinese, the bare man/woman pair mard/zan does not reverse (-0.102), although its masculine extreme does show the pattern that made that pair unreliable elsewhere, namely the generic words for a person (fard, shakhs, afrād 'individuals')-the lexical form of the androcentric default in which the generic person is a man 50 .
text.formatted: Nine of the ten single pairs are negative on their own, from dāmād/arus (-0.299) to barādar/khāhar (-0.093); unlike in Dutch, Estonian and Chinese, the bare man/woman pair mard/zan does not reverse (-0.102), although its masculine extreme does show the pattern that made that pair unreliable elsewhere, namely the generic words for a person (fard, shakhs, afrād 'individuals')-the lexical form of the androcentric default in which the generic person is a man <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">50</ref> .

text.text: The one reversed pair is amu/amme (0.131), and its extremes show that it is not a gender axis at all: they are everyday nouns unrelated to gender (enteshār 'publication', otāq 'room', khāb 'sleep' at one end; sabz 'green', barg 'leaf', kārtun 'cartoon' at the other), consistent with amu doubling as a familiar term of address for any adult man in children's speech.
Averaging over several pairs removes this pair-specific variance, as in the other languages.
The words at the two extremes again show the bias in a direct form, with a different emphasis from Chinese.

The feminine extreme of the primary axis consists of words for women (zan 'woman', bānu 'lady', khānom 'Ms', malake 'queen') and, prominently, of words for the female body, sexuality and maternity (pestān 'breast', seksi 'sexy', lokht 'naked', hāmele 'pregnant', zanāne 'feminine'); the masculine extreme consists of kinship terms (barādar, pedar, pesar) followed by titles of military, religious and social rank and by male given names (sardār 'commander', khān, jenāb 'his excellency', mollā, hāji, seyyed, āqā 'sir', Mohammad, Ali).

Women are thus represented at the feminine pole through the body and through marital and maternal states (arus 'bride', hāmele 'pregnant'), and men at the masculine pole through titles of authority and status.

This is the Persian counterpart of the asymmetries seen in Estonian (men as role nouns) and Chinese (men as the vocabulary of reasoning and command, women as women), and it speaks directly to the objectification argument of the Discussion: in each language the feminine pole is anchored in concrete, embodied referents and the masculine pole in roles, rank and abstraction.

In sum, the male abstraction bias replicates in Persian, a fourth language from a third family and a third script, with human concreteness judgements collected by a different method (best-worst scaling) and with the most stable seed-pair behaviour of the four languages.

With Dutch, Estonian and Chinese, the text-based result now holds in four languages, three of them without grammatical gender, and in every case the sign is the same whenever the gender axis is built from several unambiguous kinship and role pairs.

text.text: The two sets of norms were collected with the same instructions and rating scale, but they differ in ways that could matter for our analyses: phrases are predominantly nominal and they are less polysemous than single words.
Here we confirm that the male abstraction bias does not depend on pooling the two.

For each language model, we computed the two-tailed Pearson's correlation between the gender association of a term (positive values indicate masculine associations) and its concreteness, separately for (i) words and phrases pooled, (ii) words only and (iii) phrases only, with 95% confidence intervals obtained using the Fisher transformation.
Within each of these analyses, P values were Bonferronicorrected for the number of language models examined.

To summarize across models, we treated language models as the units of analysis: we report the unweighted mean of the per-model correlations, with a 95% confidence interval from the t distribution across models, and a two-tailed one-sample t-test of the per-model correlations against zero.
No model is weighted more heavily than any other.

text.text: For words, the mean correlation across models was -0.085 (95% CI = -0.131 to -0.039; t(11) = -4.10; P = 0.002), and the correlation was negative in 11 of 12 models (significantly so after Bonferroni correction in 11).
Terms in the most feminine decile had a mean concreteness of 3.31, compared with 3.02 for terms in the most masculine decile.

For phrases, the mean correlation was -0.252 (95% CI = -0.295 to -0.210; t(11) = -13.10; P = 4.7 × 10 -8 ), and the correlation was negative in 12 of 12 models (significantly so in 12); mean concreteness was 3.55 in the most feminine decile and 2.74 in the most masculine decile.
The one exception among single words was ConceptNet, for which the correlation was small and positive (r = 0.04; 95% CI = 0.03 to 0.05; n = 38,341 words).
The bias is thus present in both datasets but is markedly stronger for phrases than for single words.

Supplementary Section 9 shows that roughly half of this difference is accounted for by the frequency, length and part of speech of the phrases, and that the association in both datasets is robust to these and other lexical covariates.

For single words, the covariates were word frequency (log-transformed SUBTLEX-US frequency, as distributed with the concreteness norms 21 ); length, measured as the number of characters and the number of syllables (from the CMU Pronouncing Dictionary, with an orthographic approximation for words it does not contain); polysemy, measured as the log-transformed number of senses recorded for the word in WordNet 82 (n = 34,026 words with an entry); age of acquisition 117 (n = 23,860); valence, arousal and dominance 118 (n = 13,385); and the word's dominant part of speech, as recorded in the concreteness norms or, for words without one, the part of speech of the word's first WordNet sense, entered as fixed effects.

text.text: Because polysemy, age of acquisition and the affective ratings are available for subsets of the words, for these covariates we also report the association without controls on the same subset, which separates the effect of the control from the effect of the change in sample.

For phrases, frequency, age of acquisition and the affective ratings were assigned as the mean over the phrase's constituent words that appear in the respective norms; length was measured as the number of characters and the number of words; polysemy as the number of WordNet senses of the phrase itself, together with an indicator for whether the phrase has a WordNet entry (25,202 of the 62,889 phrases do); and part of speech was taken from the phrase's WordNet entry or, failing that, from its head word.

Results were summarized across models as in Supplementary Section 7: an unweighted mean of the per-model estimates, a 95% confidence interval and a one-sample t-test across models, and a count of the models in which the estimate was negative and significant after Bonferroni correction for the number of models.

We further (i) restricted the analysis to words known by at least 95% of the raters who judged their concreteness, and to words whose concreteness ratings had below-median standard deviation across raters, and (ii) estimated the association without controls separately within each quintile of word frequency.

text.text: Word frequency did not account for the association: controlling for it left the mean estimate across models essentially unchanged (mean β = -0.091; 95% CI = -0.143 to -0.039; t(11) = -3.88; P = 0.003; compared with -0.085 without controls), and the association was negative in every quintile of word frequency (mean β = -0.127 among the least frequent fifth of words, -0.096, -0.071 and -0.065 in the next three fifths, and -0.089 among the most frequent fifth).

Controlling for length strengthened the association (mean β = -0.117; 95% CI = -0.169 to -0.064), as did restricting the analysis to reliably rated words (mean β = -0.115 for words with below-median rater disagreement and -0.114 with both restrictions; negative in 11 of 12 models in each case).
Polysemy and age of acquisition made no material difference once the change in sample is taken into account.

The one covariate that attenuated the association was affective content: among the 13,385 words with affective ratings, controlling for valence, arousal and dominance reduced the mean estimate from -0.063 to -0.052 (95% CI = -0.094 to -0.010; negative in 9 of 12 models), because more positive words are both more concrete and more feminine.

Controlling for all covariates simultaneously, together with part-of-speech fixed effects, nevertheless yielded a larger estimate than the association without controls on the same words (mean β = -0.099; 95% CI = -0.143 to -0.054; t(11) = -4.90; P = 4.7 × 10 -4 ; negative in 11 of 12 models and significantly so in 10, compared with -0.063 without controls; n = 13,069 to 13,082 words per model), and controlling for frequency, length, polysemy and part of speech in the much larger set of words with a WordNet entry gave a similar estimate (mean β = -0.101; 95% CI = -0.149 to -0.053; negative in 11 of 12 models; n = 28,958 to 34,026).

Roughly half of the stronger association observed for phrases than for words in Fig. 1a therefore reflects the fact that more abstract phrases are composed of rarer words, are longer and are more often verb phrases, properties that are correlated with gender association in their own right; the remaining association, which is comparable in size to that observed for single words, is independent of these properties.

Here we show that the central within-domain result-that the most abstract third of a domain is more male-associated than its most concrete third-does not depend on this choice, or more generally on how individual words are assigned to domains.
All comparisons hold the vocabulary and the gender scores fixed and vary only domain membership, so that any difference between schemes isolates the contribution of the assignment rule.

The vocabulary comprises the 25,597 single-word entries of the concreteness norms 21 whose dominant part of speech is a noun, verb, adjective or adverb and that have at least one WordNet 82 sense in that part of speech (two-word entries carry no dominant part of speech and are excluded; WordNet's participial adjective file adj.ppl is folded into adj.all).

text.text: We then recompute the Fig. 2 quantity under each assignment scheme: within every domain containing at least 100 assigned words, words are split into terciles by their concreteness rating; the domain's gap is the mean gender association of the most abstract third minus that of the most concrete third, averaged with equal weight across the 12 models; each domain's gap is tested with a two-tailed one-sample t-test across models (df = 11), and the share of domains with a positive gap is tested with a two-tailed binomial sign test.

text.text: Four assignment schemes are compared. (i) Primary sense, the main-text rule: each word receives the single domain of its first-listed WordNet sense within its dominant part of speech. (ii) All senses, the rule of Supplementary Section 10: a word joins every domain in which it has a sense within its dominant part of speech, so a polysemous word can contribute to several domains. (iii) Domain-unambiguous words only: the analysis is restricted to the 16,553 words whose senses all fall in a single domain, for which assignment is beyond dispute and the primary/all-sense distinction vanishes. (iv) Random sense: each word receives the domain of one uniformly sampled sense within its dominant part of speech, and the entire analysis is repeated over 200 independent replicates, characterizing the full distribution of results attainable by perturbing the assignment of every polysemous word at once. without faces are not distributed evenly: more concrete terms, which more often depict objects than people, were less likely to return any faces (r = -0.25 between concreteness and whether a term returned at least one face; 95% CI = -0.25 to -0.24; P < 2.2 × 10 -16 ; n = 39,956; two-tailed Pearson's correlation).

text.text: Only 2.5% of terms in the most abstract fifth of the vocabulary returned no faces, compared with 23.8% of terms in the most concrete fifth.
The gradient in Fig. 3 therefore combines two patterns: more abstract concepts are more likely to be depicted with people at all, and, when people are depicted, they are more likely to be men.

text.text: Here we isolate the second pattern and show that it is robust.

text.text: Specification (2) examines only the terms whose images contained at least one face (n = 35,913 for concreteness; n = 35,677 for perceptual strength).

Among these terms, a one-point increase in concreteness was associated with a decrease of 1.3 percentage points in the share of male faces (r = -0.07; 95% CI = -0.08 to -0.06), and the share of male faces declined from 66.9% in the most abstract twentieth of terms to 62.1% in the most concrete twentieth; for perceptual strength, the corresponding decline was from 65.3% to 62.3% (r = -0.05; 95% CI = -0.06 to -0.04).

Men were thus the majority of faces at every level of concreteness (67.3% of the 1,211,815 faces detected overall), and the association between abstraction and male faces, although considerably smaller than in specification (1), remained highly significant.

Specifications (3)-(5) show that this association is robust to controlling for the number of faces associated with each term (log-transformed), the frequency of the term in everyday language (log-transformed SUBTLEX-US frequency, as distributed with the concreteness norms 21 ), the mean confidence of the gender classifications for the term and fixed effects for the term's dominant part of speech.

text.text: Specification (6) shows that it holds when examining only terms associated with at least ten faces, for which the fraction of male faces is measured more reliably.

Finally, specification (7) models the counts of male and female faces for each term directly, using a quasi-binomial regression that weights each term by its number of faces and allows for overdispersion; coefficients for this model are in log-odds.
Across all specifications, and for both measures, more abstract terms were associated with a significantly higher fraction of male faces.

text.text: The association shown in the main text therefore combines two components: more concrete terms are less likely to return images of people at all, and, when people are shown, a smaller fraction of them are male.

This section tests whether the second component holds on its own, that is, whether the negative association between concreteness and male representation is robust to how terms without faces are treated and to variation in the number of faces per term.

We estimated five families of models, each separately for human judgments of concreteness (Brysbaert norms; N = 39,956 terms) and for perceptual strength (Lancaster sensorimotor norms, mean of the six perceptual modalities; N = 39,707 terms).

(A) Retaining all search terms, as in the main text, we added as covariates the number of detected faces, log(1 + faces), an indicator for whether the term returned any face, and word frequency (ln(1 + SUBTLEX count)).

(B) We restricted the sample to terms with at least one detected face, for which the male fraction is defined, and then to terms with at least 5, 10 and 20 faces, for which it is measured with increasing precision.

(C) Among terms with at least one face, we used three alternative estimators: ordinary least squares weighting each term by its number of faces; a quasi-binomial logistic regression of the counts of male and female faces, which treats the face rather than the search term as the unit of observation and estimates the dispersion from the data; and the Spearman rank correlation.

text.text: Rows labelled β are standardized coefficients on concreteness from regressions of the z-scored gender score on z-scored concreteness and the covariates listed, with heteroskedasticity-robust (HC1) 95% confidence intervals; all other rows are two-tailed Pearson's correlations with Fisher-transformed intervals.
Word frequency is the log rank of the word in the fastText vocabulary, which is ordered by corpus frequency; length is the number of characters.

Standardized coefficients (β) on concreteness, summarized across models as in Supplementary Table13(Neg., number of models with a negative coefficient; in parentheses, the number that were also significant after Bonferroni correction).

Rows exclude person nouns, lexically gendered terms, function words and proper names (for phrases, person nouns and lexically gendered terms), with and without controls for frequency, length and part of speech; exclude the 5% or 10% of terms with the most extreme gender association (|z|) within each model; report Spearman's rank correlation; and report, for each model, the least negative estimate obtained when omitting each WordNet domain (with at least 100 terms) in turn.
Fig 1a replicates in Persian.

Across the 2,924 human-rated words, more masculine words are more abstract (r = -0.194; 95% CI = -0.228 to -0.158; P < 2.2 × 10 -16 ; Spearman's ρ = -0.191), and mean concreteness falls from 0.58 in the most feminine decile to 0.47 in the ninth decile, with 0.49 in the most masculine.
text.formatted: Across the 2,924 human-rated words, more masculine words are more abstract (r = -0.194; 95% CI = -0.228 to -0.158; P < 2.2 × 10 -16 ; Spearman's ρ = -0.191), and mean concreteness falls from 0.58 in the most feminine decile to 0.47 in the ninth decile, with 0.49 in the most masculine.

text.text: The difference between the extreme deciles is 0.087 on the 0-1 scale, or 0.65 s.d. of the ratings; between the first and ninth deciles it is 0.86 s.d.
The extended axis gives r = -0.208 (-0.243 to -0.173; ρ = -0.216) and a difference of 0.71 s.d. between the extreme deciles.

In units of the ratings' standard deviation the Persian effect is thus the largest after Dutch (0.84 s.d.) and above the Estonian (0.37 s.d.) and Chinese (0.38 s.d.) estimates, and the correlation lies between the Chinese and Dutch ones; its confidence interval is wider than in the other languages because the human-rated set is smaller.
